#1803. England’s potential path to glory proves Nations League is more difficult to win than the World Cup

Sometimes you have to say the unsayable because no one else will.

The Nations League is a more difficult competition to win than the World Cup or the European Championships. Stay with me.

Though there remain plenty of club football fans who take no interest in international football outside of major tournaments and are sceptical about the Nations League, there has been a noticeable drop in the number of club fans repeating the trite notion it is a pointless competition made up of glorified friendlies no one cares about.

My hunch as to why: people are beginning to realise how much of a refreshing addition to the football it really is, plus how many tasty fixtures it produces. And it is that final point — the competition regularly throwing up blockbuster clashes between European heavyweights — that explains why the Nations League might just be the hardest competition to win in international football.

A disclaimer is needed at this point. The Nations League is not a major tournament like the World Cup or European Championships are. Those competitions take place in single block international breaks during the summer (except when hosted in the Middle East) and the stakes at play mean immeasurably more pressure and psychological challenges as players and teams seek to win the trophies that matter most.

The World Cup and Euros remain more psychologically draining and patently more important. But more difficult to win than the Nations League in a footballing sense? Honestly, no.

The calibre of opposition is far higher in Europe’s newest event compared with the World Cup or Euros. Just look at Argentina’s route to the World Cup final where they were defeated by Spain.

They faced Algeria, Austria, debutants Jordan, fellow debutants Cape Verde, Egypt, Switzerland and then finally one world-football powerhouse, England, and were suddenly into a World Cup final.

For all their memories of their best World Cup finish since 1966, England’s route to their semi-final defeat to Argentina was not much more difficult. Croatia, Ghana, Panama, DR Congo, Mexico, and finally Norway.

And in their previous tournament, when England limped to the Euro 2024 final under Gareth Southgate with a string of uninspiring performances, they faced Serbia, Denmark, Slovenia, Slovakia, Switzerland and the Netherlands — and navigating that pretty presentable route meant they had qualified for the final and a shot at becoming European champions.

And what made this summer’s expanded World Cup even less likely to produce those big fixtures was FIFA’s brazenly cynical introduction of Wimbledon-styled protected ranking at its seeding stage.

The world’s four top-ranked nations would be kept apart in different quarters of the draw until the semi-finals providing they each won their groups. Shock: they all did.

Sure enough, for the first time in history the four top ranks made up the men’s World Cup semi-finalists: Argentina, England, France and Spain. A great product, just as FIFA wanted, but it had taken 100 matches to get there, the only blockbuster fixture among 72 group matches having been Spain and Uruguay, two former winners.

Winter energy bill misery on way as price cap set to jump by 26% in January

England’s Ivan Toney fails in bid to move assault trial over Euro 2028 clash

Nations League draw simulated as England get favourable quarter-final tie

Discover a hidden island paradise in the Indian Ocean

The World Cup was great, but plenty of its matches had been rather too easy to call beforehand.

The calibre of opposition is far higher in Europe’s newest event compared with the World Cup or Euros

Now consider England’s potential path to Nations League glory next summer. A group stage first of all where England faced Czechia, Croatia and world champions Spain home and away.

Croatia are a good footballing nation but by finishing third of the group are now out, with next March to bring together only the winners and runners up from the four groups for the quarter-finals.

Group A3 winners England will face either Belgium, the Netherlands or Erling Haaland’s Norway — the teams ranked eighth, ninth and 19th in the world rankings.

After a two-legged tie against one of those opponents, England would gear up for next summer’s Nations League Finals, a one-off semi-final and then potentially a final, with France, Germany or Portugal as their likeliest opponents in those two games.

Here is a string of prestige fixtures far more testing for Thomas Tuchel’s side than the World Cup produced. No comparison in pressure and scrutiny, granted, but tougher in purely footballing terms, undoubtedly — and coaches are not rotating their teams or resting players as much as one might imagine. It is taken seriously.

For its sheer hit rate of big games out of the total set of fixtures and for how consistently well a top team would have to perform to navigate them all, the UEFA Nations League has become international football’s most difficult competition to win. There. Sometimes you have to say the unsayable because no one else will.

#1802. Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United: Will Things Finally Change at Old Trafford?

When Mauricio Pochettino walks into Anfield for his first match as Manchester United manager, he will immediately be confronted by the scale of the challenge ahead. There are easier ways to begin a reign than an away trip to Liverpool, especially for a club that has spent much of the past decade searching for stability and finding very little of it.

The symbolism is obvious. Liverpool have spent recent years building coherent teams, developing clear identities and competing regularly for major trophies, even if they did hit a few bumps on the road themselves. Manchester United have spent the same period cycling through managers, rebuilding projects and tactical resets. Pochettino’s appointment represents another attempt to break that pattern, but it would be a mistake to believe the Argentine’s task begins and ends with improving results.

His predecessors discovered that managing the team is only part of the job. The harder challenge is changing the culture and structure of a club that has repeatedly undermined its own attempts at renewal.

Pochettino was right to push back against the idea that Manchester United’s problems can be reduced to distance covered or sprint numbers.

The statistics are alarming. United have been outrun in most of their league matches and rank near the bottom of the division in several physical metrics. Yet simply demanding greater effort is unlikely to transform a struggling team overnight.

What United have lacked for years is collective purpose. Too often the team has looked like a group of talented individuals operating with different interpretations of the same game plan. When Pochettino talks about players running together and understanding their roles, he is really describing something more fundamental than fitness. He is talking about creating a collective identity.

That was one of the defining strengths of his best Tottenham side. They were physically outstanding, but their success came from organisation and belief as much as athleticism. Every player understood what was expected of him, and the team functioned as a coherent unit.

Manchester United have not consistently looked like that under any manager for a very long time.

It’s official. Mauricio is a Red 🔴📸 https://t.co/9uq47U3S3Z

— Manchester United (@ManUtd) November 18, 2026

The obvious counterargument is that other highly regarded coaches have arrived at Old Trafford with similarly ambitious ideas.

Erik ten Hag was respected throughout Europe. Ruben Amorim arrived with a reputation as one of the continent’s brightest tactical minds. Others before them possessed impressive credentials too.

What makes Pochettino different is the nature of his previous achievements.

Unlike some elite managers, he has rarely inherited finished products. His reputation was built on developing teams, improving players and creating environments where younger footballers could thrive. His Tottenham side became one of Europe’s best teams despite operating with fewer resources than many of their rivals, while his spell at Chelsea demonstrated an ability to stabilise a chaotic dressing room and extract improvement from a talented but unbalanced squad.

That experience feels particularly relevant at Manchester United. This is not a club requiring minor adjustments; it is a club still searching for a clear football identity. Pochettino has spent much of his career building exactly that.

Even the best coaches struggle when recruitment and management pull in different directions, and that, among other things is where Manchester United have repeatedly run into trouble.

Successive managers have inherited squads constructed for different styles of football. Players signed for one coach have remained when another arrived with entirely different ideas. The result has been an increasingly awkward collection of footballers who often appear unsuited to the system being asked of them.

If Pochettino is to succeed, that cycle cannot continue.

The club’s hierarchy must show the discipline to recruit according to a long-term strategy rather than chasing short-term fixes. That requires difficult decisions, particularly regarding players who may still carry reputations but no longer fit the demands of modern elite football.

Tottenham’s rise under Pochettino was possible because the squad gradually became an extension of the manager’s ideas. Manchester United have not reached that point under any coach since Sir Alex Ferguson.

Without alignment between the manager and recruitment department, even the strongest project stalls, and eventually fails.

Perhaps the greatest danger is expecting immediate transformation.

The temptation after years of disappointment will be to judge Pochettino’s reign through the lens of short-term results. That is understandable, especially when the club sits far below the standards many expect from them.

Yet rebuilding rarely follows a straight line. Pochettino’s first Tottenham team finished fifth before progressing into genuine title challengers, and Champions League finalists. Many of the players who later became stars required time and patience. The same principle is likely to apply at Old Trafford.

His opening fixture at Liverpool serves as a reminder of how much work remains to be done. Whatever happens at Anfield, it should not define the project. The more important question is whether United begin to look like a team with direction.

For all the doom that surrounds Manchester United, the club remains one of football’s great institutions. The fanbase remains enormous, the resources remain substantial, and the attraction of the badge has not disappeared yet.

Pochettino himself acknowledged that reality when discussing the scale of the support he encounters around the world. That is why the job continues to draw elite managerial candidates despite the obvious risks. The potential rewards remain extraordinary. The challenge is converting potential into reality.

The honest answer is yes, but only under conditions that have often been absent at Manchester United.

Pochettino has the coaching pedigree. He has the experience of handling demanding environments. He has a proven track record of improving players and building teams. Whether that is enough depends largely on whether the club has learned from the mistakes that consumed previous managers.

If United continue changing direction every couple of years, no coach will succeed. If they provide Pochettino with time, authority and recruitment aligned to a coherent football vision, then he may have a better chance than most of restoring the club to relevance at the top of the Premier League.

His first game – away to Liverpool – is obviously a daunting introduction to the task ahead. In many ways, it will be a good indicator of where Manchester United currently stand. They are beginning another chapter while measuring themselves against a rival that has spent years getting the fundamentals right.

Pochettino’s challenge is not simply to win matches. It is to ensure that, a few years from now, Manchester United are finally discussing how to compete for titles again rather than debating the future of yet another manager.

#1801. Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

The visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU

Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.

“I think it is a really harsh one. He [the referee] has to be sure at such a critical time of the game. And I do not think he can be sure. I think he has almost had a guess that he is in the box. It is such a big call.”

“We see the ref’s position. The fact the ref makes the decision to give the penalty in my opinion, it is a bigger decision to give it then to not. We have got the luxury of the replays and we are still not sure. His whole body is outside the box.”

“It looks outside the box to me [the penalty incident]. The still picture suggests to me it was outside the box. We can get better and we will have to. We have to be more dominant with the ball at times and be better in attack. We have done a lot of work on that in pre-season. Having been in this league a long time, the power of the dressing room is crucial and any motivation tool you can you use is important. I think we will be fine. You have to enjoy football and love it. I think the boys enjoyed it tonight.”

“Obviously frustrated. The boys did everything to get the three points but it is gutting in the end. I thought I was outside the box when the ball came in and the decision went against us. They are saying it is in the box and it is frustrating. We dug deep and thought we had it. I cannot fault everyone as we all put in a shift, it was just the final details with the penalty decision. We deserved the three points. If we play like that every week, we will go far in the table.”

Bentley spills the corner but gets a free-kick. Moments later, the referee blows his whistle for the final time and the game ends level at 2-2. A dramatic opening night of the new Championship season at Molineux. If the Championship continues in this vein all season, it will be one hell of a year.

Blackburn nearly score a late winner as Garrett’s shot is tipped over the bar by Bentley for a later Blackburn corner.

He sends Toth the wrong way and calmly slots home to bring Wolves level in added time. That penalty decision will certainly create some debate. The Championship is always full of drama and we get some on opening night.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU

It just had to be. Jimenez rescues Wolves from the penalty spot.

Drama on the opening night of the campaign.

Relief for Wolves, heartbreak for Blackburn.

Late drama at Molineux! The cross is sent in from the left and the ball strikes the arm Alebiosu on the edge of the box. Was it inside or outside the penalty area? It is definitely handball but was it outside the box? It was very, very close but there is no VAR in the Championship so the penalty will stand.

Four added minutes. Are we on the verge of seeing the first shock of the new Championship season on opening night?

Four minutes added. Not even a reaction from the home crowd.

Wolves are desperately running out of time and Blackburn still look comfortable.

Home fans are beginning to filter out slowly.

Mosquera is still struggling but he has come back on whilst limping around. I cannot imagine there will be too much in terms of added time, either three or four minutes would be my guess, no more.

Ohashi is played in behind and goes down under a challenge from Toti on the edge of the Wolves box but those appeals are waved away.

Mosquera has gone down again and he may not be able to continue as he receives treatment on the sidelines. Wolves may be ending this game down to 10 men.

Fevrier’s shot from outside the Wolves penalty area is blocked and spins behind for a corner in front of the travelling Blackburn fans. The corner comes to nothing.

Wolves struggling to create anything of note even with Jimenez’s introduction.

Centre-back Mosquera has gone up front but appears to be struggling with an injury. He’s jogged back to his natural position now.

Desperate long balls being sent forward but Blackburn look comfortable for now. The home fans are quite audibly unhappy with this second-half showing.

Wolves do not currently look like scoring an equaliser.

Mosquera is struggling with a knock but Wolves made all five changes. If he is unable to continue, Wolves will have to finish off with ten men.

The frustration inside Molineux is growing and the home fans want to see some more urgency from their side as they trail with under 10 minutes left.

Blackburn are now going to make their final two alterations of the night as Ribeiro and Garrett come on.

Wolves are going to make their final two substitutions as Lima and Chirewa replace Moller Wolfe and Andre.

Blackburn are looking pretty comfortable right now defending their lead and counter-attacking effectively.

Wolves want a penalty as Armstrong goes down inside the box after making a run in behind but the appeals are waved away. Rightly so as Armstrong was not fouled.

Wolves are pushing to find an equaliser but are struggling to carve out many genuine opportunities.

Ohashi is penalised for a foul on F Lopez not far outside the Blackburn penalty area and that was pretty harsh on Ohashi. Jimenez is lining this one up as is F Lopez.

The former takes but his effort hits the wall.

Wolves’ frustration right now is summed up by a dreadful cross from F Lopez from the right side of the box that goes behind for a goal kick. The TV cameras then turn to some of the Wolves fans, who look rather forlorn in the stands.

Double changes for both sides. For Wolves, Doyle and Tchatchoua come on. For Blackburn, Fevrier and Ohasi enter the fray.

You’d have thought a goal had gone in such is the reaction from the home crowd to Jimenez’s introduction. I have to say, I’m surprised Mane has made way but Jimenez will play through the middle with Armstrong moved out to the left.

Blackburn made a change earlier in the half with Wolverhampton-born Sam Morsy on for his Rovers debut. One manager going for it as the other attempts to shore things up.

Wolves’ last shot on target was all the way back in the 18th minute, when Munetsi put them in front. That is in fact their only shot on target tonight, compared to Blackburn’s four.

Should Wolves have been given a penalty? Jimenez goes down after Atcheson did stick out his leg but was there enough in it to give a penalty?

Jimenez is indeed now going to come on and Molineux rises to welcome him onto the pitch. The Jimenez scarfs go up around the ground and his song is sung. Mane goes off.

Raúl Jiménez receives an incredible reception from the Wolves fans as he makes his league return for the club 👏🇲🇽 pic.twitter.com/mPE7pvTJZt

No messing about from new Wolves boss Cesar Peixoto with his side behind and discontent brewing in the stands, Raul Jimenez is going to be introduced. His name has been sung throughout the game with a hero’s welcome imminent.

Can he inspire a comeback? Wolves and Peixoto will certainly hope so.

Munetsi, the scorer of Wolves’ goal, has a shot deflected from the edge of the box and it goes behind for a corner. Gudjohnsen, the scorer of Blackburn’s second, heads away at the front post.

You can sense the frustration growing from the home fans inside Molineux, with a few groans creeping in.

Blackburn are the first to turn to their bench as one experienced midfielder replaces another with Morsy coming on for Forshaw.

Wow! What a start to the second half. Blackburn have turned it around, Tony Mowbray clearly inspired his troops at half time.

Molineux is silenced now with Blackburn fans making all the noise. Some home supporters were still taking their seats as Gudjohnsen turned the ball home.

Can Wolves turn the game back in their favour? It’s all a bit slow now from the hosts followed by the first signs of disgruntlement from the home supporters.

And to top it off, Mane is booked for simulation.

The first Wolves player into the book tonight is Mane and it is for simulation. Watching the replays, that feels like a fair call as Mane threw himself to the ground and it probably was a dive.

Molineux is stunned as the underdogs take the lead inside the opening five minutes of the second half. Tony Mowbray’s side have started well since the break and are rewarded. Afolayan is found making a run into the penalty area on the right side of the box and his cross is slotted home by Gudjohnsen. His father Eidur would have been happy with a striker’s finish like that.

Morishita drives forward through the Wolves half and towards the penalty area. He lays it off to Afolayan, whose effort is tipped over the bar by Bentley for a Blackburn corner, which is headed and then cleared away by Wolves.

We are back under way at Molineux. No changes for either side at the break.

An intriguing first half as the whistle sounds and both teams head down the tunnel.

Both teams scored when the other seemed on top slightly.

Wolves have probably shaded it with those efforts from Lopez and Mane which went narrowly over.

Plenty to think about for the two managers.

The first half is brought to a close at Molineux and an engaging opening 45 minutes of the new Championship season results in this game being level at 1-1 at the break. Munetsi put Wolves in front before McLoughlin equalised for Blackburn.

Forshaw is the third Blackburn player into the book tonight as the referee goes back to penalise the midfielder for an earlier foul on Andre. That was not Forshaw’s first foul either.

With no VAR or hydration breaks, there will be just one added minute at the end of this first half.

Mane wins it back for his side on the edge of his own penalty area and drives forward. He takes it across the halfway line before feeding a lovely pass to his right to find Armstrong, whose shot is blocked.

Mane comes close to a stunner. Trippier rolls the ball across the face of the penalty area to 18-year-old Mane, who takes on the shot first time but his effort goes just over the bar.

Wolves come close to restoring their lead. Mane drives inside from the left and plays the ball forward to F Lopez, who takes one touch before getting his shot away from just outside the box. He tries to pick out the top corner but it just misses the target.

Like London buses, two yellow cards come at once and another Blackburn player is into the book. It is their captain Cantwell who receives a yellow card for delaying the restart. Cantwell was not too impressed with that decision.

Both teams off the mark for the season now, a brilliant near-post run and header from McLoughlin who scores his first-ever goal in English football to level the game up.

Molineux briefly stunned into silence. A slight delay from the fans celebrating the header as well.

The first booking of the Championship season goes the way of Blackburn left-back Pickering. It is a pretty simple decision for the referee as Pickering cynically pulls back R Gomes, who had spun him, and rightly receives a yellow card.

R Gomes delivers a cross from the right side of the Blackburn box across the penalty area but Armstrong does not pre-empt that and is not on hand to meet it. However, Alebiosu, with Mane not far behind him, puts it behind for a corner. Trippier delivers and the Blackburn keeper makes a meal of it, missing his punch out but then scrambles back towards his own goal to gather the loose ball.

The visitors went behind against the run of play but probably deservedly they are back on level terms. Morishita clips in the cross from the right to the near post, where McLoughlin meets it first and guides a powerful header into the far corner. Two goals in the opening half an hour of the new Championship season.

"They STUN Molineux!" 😳Sean Mcloughlin delightfully heads past Dan Bentley to equalise for Blackburn 👏 pic.twitter.com/v5qLhJ0wBt

Blackburn are getting great joy down their right through Alebiosu and Morishita, with the latter winning them a corner as Toti is forced to head behind from a cross. Pickering sends it into a good area and the touch comes off the head of Munetsi, whose header loops into the air and goes just over his own bar for another corner on the other side.

Cantwell’s delivery to the far post is headed away.

We have the first goal of the season and it’s the returning Marshall Munetsi who gets it.

A cool finish from the midfielder after a bit of a drab start from the home side.

That will please the new Wolves boss. Such a simple move but the home side ripped Blackburn wide open with two passes.

Work to do for the visitors now who had probably started the better of the two teams before the opener.

Wolves fans make their feelings about VAR known following the goal. No VAR in the Championship of course but no VAR was needed for that anyway. A perfectly good goal.

Mane cuts inside from the left onto his preferred right foot and curls a dangerous ball into the box that is punched away by Toth in the Blackburn goal. 18-year-old Mane was one of very few bright spots for Wolves last season and in many ways it is a surprise that no Premier League teams have lured him back to the top flight quite yet. That could though still happen before the deadline.

The first goal of the Championship season comes against the run of play. It is a clinical, ruthless goal that comes from an incisive pass and clinical finish. The pass is fed through by F Lopez to pick out the run of Munetsi, who is cool, calm and collected as he finishes past Toth. Blackburn had been the better side up until that point but Wolves take the lead at Molineux.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq

A shot on target for Blackburn but an easy save in the end. Alebiosu, who has looked good in these early stages, drives down Blackburn’s right before cutting it back to Morishita on the edge of the box. Morishita takes one touch before shooting but his effort is tame and straight at Bentley.

Blackburn have definitely been the better side in these early exchanges, dominating possession and looking a threat going forward.

Blackburn may be heavy underdogs tonight but they have settled down well away at one of the favourites to get promoted. Tony Mowbray may well be seeing this as a good time to play Wolves away.

Alebiosu shows quick feet down Blackburn’s right and clips a cross to the back post, where Afolayan meets it but his header is just off target.

Safe to say the doom and gloom of last season appears to have lifted at Molineux. The home fans in fine voice early on here.

By contrast, Kieran Trippier’s first touch of the season is greeted by loud boos by the travelling Blackburn supporters.

In fact, every Trippier touch is greeted by a chorus of boos. Will they keep that up all game?

They’ve certainly not forgotten his Burnley connection.

New managers and new signings galore. This should be a fascinating spectacle.

He may not be in the starting XI tonight but Jimenez is being serenaded by the home fans on his return to Wolves after a few years away at Fulham. Jimenez and his wife have paid for 5,000 scarves for the Wolves fans tonight.

Blackburn boss Tony Mowbray did say ahead of the game that Wolves have not been used to winning games over the last 12 months so can the visitors take advantage of that tonight? Blackburn are underdogs tonight and not too much is expected of them this season so surely they have nothing to lose this evening?

Due to his Burnley ties, new Wolves defender Trippier is booed by the travelling Blackburn fans. On the other side of defence for Wolves is Moller Wolfe, who started for Norway against England in the World Cup quarter-finals in Miami.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off on opening night in the Championship.

When Wolverhampton Wanderers last attacked the Championship under a Portuguese manager new to English football, it proved a vintage season.

Molineux was under the spell of Nuno Espírito Santo in that 2017-18 campaign, and the big question is whether César Peixoto can lead a repeat nearly a decade later.

Peixoto was a surprise appointment in June, replacing Rob Edwards, and he has been entrusted with the mission of returning Wolves to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

“I have changed some things with set-pieces and some things in other moments of the game because I want the team to be organised and understand all the different moments within a match. During pre-season we have scored some goals from high pressing, but we will not be able to press high in every moment of every game. The players have to understand the game and recognise what each moment requires. It is important that we work as a team. When we can press high, we’ll press high. When we need to defend in a mid-block, we will stay organised. When the opposition pushes us deeper, which will sometimes happen, we have to be organised there as well.

“There are a lot of crosses in the Championship, for example, so the team needs to understand what to do in those situations. We want to play our football, be offensive and react strongly when we lose the ball, but we also need to understand the different moments of the game. I think we are at a good level to attack the Championship.”

Our experts have been having their say ahead of the new Championship season. A number of them believe Wolves will be promoted, including John Percy:

It is difficult to look beyond West Ham. Nuno Espírito Santo romped to the Championship title with Wolves in 2018 and remains a shrewd operator (along with his No 2 Rui Pedro Silva), while convincing Jarrod Bowen to stay is significant. I am going to go for Wolves and Middlesbrough as the other two promoted clubs.

The 2026/27 Championship season kicks off at Molineux as Wolves host Blackburn, with the home side hoping to put the bad memories of last season firmly behind them. There are new playoff rules in place for this season, with six places now up for grabs in the play-offs.

Wolves are aiming to return to the Premier League at the first attempt, having endured a miserable season in the top flight last year as they finished bottom with just three wins to their name. It has been a summer of change at the club as they chose to change managers. Rob Edwards lost his job in what was a shock move and was replaced by 46-year-old Cesar Peixoto, with this being his first head coaching position outside of his home country Portugal. Back in 2017/18, Wolves won the Championship title led by Peixoto’s compatriot Nuno Espirito Santo.

“I am ready,” Peixoto told Wolves’ club website. “We have worked very hard during pre-season, and I think we have had a great pre-season. All the players have worked very, very hard and they understand what I want from them. I am ready and confident going into the first game. Football is football, whether it is in Portugal or England, but there are different characteristics to the game here. We have watched, observed and analysed the Championship. We did that work before I came to the club, so we know what to expect.

“It is going to be a tough season with good teams, but we are prepared to fight for the three points game after game and week after week. We know what we want from the team and we know what our big goal is. We’re going to work very hard and fight to achieve that goal.”

They have brought in vast experience on the player side in the shape of Kieran Trippier and Raul Jimenez, who is back at Molineux three years after leaving for Fulham. Although they have lost Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes to Aston Villa, most of their squad has stayed intact as they pursue promotion back to the top flight. It is a special year for the club as they celebrate their 150th anniversary.

Blackburn, led by experienced manager Tony Mowbray, did not enjoy a great season in the Championship last year, finishing down in 20th place and just five points above the relegation zone. 14 years have now passed since Blackburn last played in the top flight.

“I think it is a tough start,” Mowbray said. “On paper, I would suggest the first couple of games, particularly, jumped out as a tough start. One of the Premier League sides from last season, away from home. They have got a very talented squad, a pretty expensive squad. They have got some very good individual talent. Yet, there is an argument to say they have not won many football matches in the last calendar year. So, what we get, we will have to wait and see.”

These sides last met in the FA Cup during the 2024/25 season, with Wolves winning that fourth-round tie 2-0 thanks to goals from Matheus Cunha and Gomes, both of whom are now plying their trade elsewhere. The omens would appear to be on Wolves’ side as they are unbeaten in their last eight league meetings with Blackburn. Both sides progressed to the second round of the League Cup last weekend, with Wolves beating Port Vale 3-0 and Blackburn overcoming Burton Albion 2-1.

#1800. Chelsea injury news: Moises Caicedo concern grows after Ecuador half-time withdrawal

By Darren Plant | 18 Nov 2026 09:30

Moises Caicedo has remained as an injury doubt for Chelsea's Premier League fixture with Leeds United on Saturday afternoon.

Despite Xabi Alonso acknowledging that the midfielder was carrying a fitness issue into the game at Sunderland before the November international break, Caicedo played the full 90 minutes at the Stadium of Light.

Prior to representing his country across two matches, the Blues star himself admitted that he was not fully fit, yet intended to feature in both games.

As well as playing 84 minutes against Costa Rica at the weekend, Caicedo featured for 45 minutes versus Bolivia on Tuesday night.

However, it has since been revealed that the 25-year-old requested to be withdrawn at half time.

Speaking to reporter Johanna Calderon after the Bolivia match, Caicedo suggested that he did not want to risk his fitness in the second half.

In an video posted on X, he said: "I wasn’t feeling too well, so I asked to come off.

"I have another commitment with my club, so I’m trying to get there as soon as possible and recover."

Not only does Caicedo now face a long-haul flight from Ecuador, he is giving up five hours of recovery due to the time difference between Guayaquil and London.

When you factor in tiredness to add to the injury issue that he is currently trying to protect, Caicedo should not be starting the game with Leeds.

Jordan Henderson was not called up by England, whereas Romeo Lavia played on Sunday night having missed Belgium's first of two UEFA Nations game during the international break.

Starting that pair and having Caicedo on the substitutes' bench is the only scenario that makes sense for Alonso.

#1799. Why Manchester United kit selection vs Liverpool could be a good omen - with one glaring exception

Mauricio Pochettino has potentially been handed a positive omen for his first game in charge of Manchester United.

The Argentine begins his tenure as Red Devils boss with the daunting prospect of facing the club’s biggest rivals away from home, with the two sides in contrasting form.

Pochettino arrives at a club currently in the bottom three of the Premier League, while Andoni Iraola has Liverpool fourth in the Premier League table after 10 games.

For Sunday’s trip to Anfield, Man United have confirmed they will wear this season’s third kit which consists of white shirts and black shorts.

Interestingly, Man Utd’s four most recent victories at the home of their arch rivals have come with the players wearing white shirts, including the away half of last season’s double.

Harry Maguire’s header late on gave Man United a 2-1 win at Anfield, ending a run of 10 games without a win for Man United at Anfield.

To find further wins in white for Manchester United at Anfield you would have to go back to Louis van Gaal’s reign.

In 2016 Wayne Rooney’s strike sealed a smash-and-grab 1-0 win against Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool, with Juan Mata starring the year prior.

However, fans will recall that Man United wore white when they were embarrassed 7-0 at Anfield in March 2023.

Coincidentally, Man Utd are undefeated at Anfield since that humbling loss, picking up two draws and a win in their last three visits to Liverpool. On those occasions Man Utd wore all white.

There was a large gap between white strips for Manchester United on trips to Anfield, with a six-year wait between a 2-0 defeat in the Europa League in 2016 and a 4-0 hammering in 2022.

#1797. ‘It’s a privilege’: Mauricio Pochettino’s first words as Manchester United manager

Mauricio Pochettino has spoken for the first time after officially starting work as Manchester United manager.

Pochettino was announced as the new Man United head coach last week, replacing Michael Carrick, but his arrival at Carrington had been delayed due to finishing up with the United States Men’s National Team [USMNT].

The Argentine bowed out of international management by overseeing a 2-0 win for USA against Haiti in the early hours on Wednesday.

After fulfilling his post-match media obligations, Pochettino flew directly from Cincinnati to the UK, touching down at Manchester airport before midday and then travelling to Carrington.

November 18 was always intended to be the 54-year-old’s start date and in his first interview in Man Utd colours, Pochettino said: “Very excited to be here, it's an honour, it's a privilege to be in this amazing club.

"Mauricio Pochettino has officially started work as Manchester United head coach, marking the start of a dream role for the Argentinian," a club statement reads.

"Pochettino’s appointment was announced last Friday with an agreement he’ll begin on 18 November, once he had fulfilled his duties with the US Men’s National Team.

"As Mauricio explained during a press conference last week, it was important for him to maintain complete focus on two remaining fixtures with USMNT.

"Pochettino oversaw two excellent wins over Haiti in the CONCACAF quarter finals. He then boarded a direct flight from Cincinnati to Manchester on Wednesday morning.

"Eager to get started, the 54-year-old travelled straight to Carrington to tour our training complex, meet a selection of players and staff, and begin work as our new head coach."

#1796. Manchester United confirm FIVE departures as Mauricio Pochettino overhaul begins

Manchester United have confirmed the departures of five members of staff after Mauricio Pochettino began work as the club’s new manager on Wednesday.

The Argentine was pictured arriving at Carrington for his first day in charge of the Red Devils, having flown immediately over after his final match with the United States.

The 54-year-old oversaw the USMNT’s 2-0 victory over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday before getting a flight straight over to Manchester with his long-serving assistant manager Miguel D’Agostino, who will join him at Old Trafford.

His other backroom staff have already been confirmed by United, with Toni Jimenez, Jesus Perez, Alec Scott and Sebastiano Pochettino, his son, all joining him in the north west.

The aforementioned quartet departed the US early for Old Trafford - before Tuesday’s match with Haiti - to begin work early ahead of Pochettino’s first game in charge.

He takes his new side to Anfield to face Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool on Sunday.

It does mean that the coaches that assisted Michael Carrick, Pochettino’s predecessor, have left the club, with United confirming as much on their website on Wednesday.

Jonathan Woodgate, Steve Holland, Travis Binnion, Craig Mawson and Jonny Evans were all part of the now-sacked head coach’s support crew, but it was clear that their jobs were in danger after the former midfielder’s sacking last Thursday.

Evans, the ex-United defender, was photographed leaving Carrington in his car on Thursday morning with boxes piled up behind him as he drove away, with many speculating that he had served his final day at his former club.

#1795. Chelsea injury news: Xabi Alonso in double boost ahead of Leeds United showdown

By Darren Plant | 18 Nov 2026 09:58

Chelsea have been handed a double injury boost ahead after Emiliano Martinez and Aaron Anselmino both represented Argentina on Tuesday night.

Martinez and Anselmino were called up by Lionel Scaloni despite spending weeks and months on the sidelines.

While goalkeeper Martinez had been unavailable with a fractured jaw since October 17, Anselmino has not played any competitive minutes for Chelsea in 2026-27 due to a hamstring injury.

However, the pair featured as Argentina cruised to a 7-0 victory over Costa Rica in Cordoba.

Starting between the sticks wearing a protective mask, Martinez played the full 90 minutes, albeit only having to make two saves during a one-sided contest.

Meanwhile, Anselmino was introduced as a 71st-minute substitute as the former world champions saw out the win.

Anselmino's outing - his first for Argentina - is particularly notable because it is his first since a 29-minute appearance in a pre-season friendly versus Johor DT on August 9.

When Moises Caicedo has provided a further fitness concern for Xabi Alonso, having Martinez and Anselmino come through unscathed for Argentina is a welcome boost.

Alonso must now decide whether to retain Mike Penders for Saturday's Premier League game with Leeds United or hand an immediate recall to Martinez.

Given the time difference and Penders having largely impressed in his absence, Martinez may expect to be named on the substitutes' bench.

Although it is possible that Anselmino will not feature in Chelsea's squad versus Leeds, Alonso requires an extra central-defensive option due to Maxence Lacroix being expected to be sidelined until January.

Realistically, the 21-year-old could be handed a start for the Blues' Under-21s ranks before coming into contention for the first team.

#1794. Ex-Manchester United star calls for ‘change at the top’ amid Mauricio Pochettino verdict

Ashley Young believes Manchester United will continue to struggle until the club changes the way it is run, while he is also unsure whether Mauricio Pochettino will have enough time to implement his ideas.

United announced the appointment of Pochettino on a two-and-a-half-year deal to succeed Michael Carrick this week, with the former Tottenham and Chelsea boss set to take his first training session on Thursday.

Pochettino becomes the fourth permanent manager to take the reins at Old Trafford since INEOS and Sir Jim Ratcliffe bought a minority stake and took over the day-to-day running of United in February 2024.

Upon buying a 27.5 per cent stake in the club, Ratcliffe insisted United needed to put a stop to the managerial turnover that had become commonplace since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013.

Yet just over two-and-a-half years on, nothing has changed, with Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick all being shown the door.

Pochettino has a huge task on his hands, with United currently sitting in the relegation zone, and Young believes that even if results initially improve, significant change won’t occur until changes are made in the boardroom.

“This season has been tough. I've said that Michael Carrick worked miracles last season with the squad that was there,” Young tells Standard Sport.

“Do I think things still need to change? Yeah, I think until things change from the top down to the manager, (United will continue to struggle). I think that things might start well, but there's always going to be some issues there.”

Pochettino has been on United’s radar for several years, and he came close to taking the head coach role on a number of occasions over the last decade before eventually agreeing to take over from Carrick.

Revered for his time in charge of Tottenham between 2014 and 2019, Pochettino has since struggled to replicate the same success he enjoyed in north London, and he leaves the US men’s national team having met rather than exceeded expectations at the World Cup this summer.

United will be aware they are not appointing the same Pochettino they courted in 2016, when the Argentine was heavily linked with the role after Louis van Gaal’s departure, and have therefore handed him a short-term deal.

This season has been tough. I've said that Michael Carrick worked miracles last season with the squad that was there

Young, though, is not sure whether Pochettino will have enough time to instil his ideas and stabilise the club after a disastrous start to the season.

“I think Mauricio Pochettino has probably gone in and said that he wants reassurances that he's going to get the players in and get the players out that he needs,” Young continued.

“But if you look at, especially when he was at Tottenham, it took him two or three years to rebuild that side. He got players in that were hungry, that wanted to play for him.

“I think if you talk to players that have played for him, it's going to be tough, it's going to be hard. So I think there's going to be a rebuild there.

“But also, he's been given a two-and-a-half-year contract. At Tottenham, it was three years to rebuild the team.

“So I think that's interesting in itself. Hopefully things can go better and go well, and the club can be stabilised. But I still think that something needs to change at the top.”

Young was speaking ahead of the launch of the Panini Official EFL Sticker Collection and said his first memories of collecting the stickers came as a kid at school.

“I always said that, you know, when you used to open packs and get a shiny (sticker), it was the best feeling ever. It was like Christmas come all over again.

“First memories of swapping at school as well. Kids at break time were like, ‘have you got this, have you got that?’ Trying to get the best ones.”

#1793. Manchester United handed transfer boost as ‘talks begin’ for Barcelona star

Manchester United could well have the chance to sign Alejandro Balde from Barcelona in January.

The Red Devils are desperate for cover at left-back with Luke Shaw and Patrick Dorgu both hampered by injury, and Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot, both natural right-backs, used in that position as deputies.

Mauricio Pochettino has started work as United’s new manager and will be looking to reinforce his options come the upcoming winter transfer window, but it remains to be seen how far he is backed so early.

Balde, 23, has previously been linked with a move to Old Trafford, but is thought to have turned down an exit from Barcelona, citing his desire to prove himself to manager Hansi Flick.

The La Masia academy product has struggled for game time this term, and could now be looking at a departure, but this time on loan.

RAC claims that the player’s agent, Jorge Mendes, is holding conversations with Barcelona about his position and a potential move, with a loan deal not out of the question.

The sticking point with a loan move is how much the loaning club will pay of the player’s wages, and it is thought that Barca could be open to an agreement where then Premier League side wouldn’t have to pay a significant share of Balde’s salary.

It is belived that the La Liga club are so desperate to let the defender leave - so they can free up space in their wage budget for new signings - that they could agree to a deal that would favour United considerably.

#1791. Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

Jaissle’s team found their feet as the first 45 minutes progressed, with Yoane Wissa their biggest attacking threat. The striker endured a difficult first season at the club, but his performances at the World Cup with DR Congo appear to have restored confidence.

Newcastle were level just before half-time, when Malick Thiaw rose highest to plant home a back-post header from a corner. Former Brentford goalkeeper Mark Flekken appealed in vain for a foul, but there was no infringement.

After changing all 10 outfield players at half-time against Everton, Jaissle was more circumspect with second-half substitutes; Rory Finneran for Lewis Miley was the only change before the 80th minute.

Newcastle faded though, and the game was won by Victor Boniface scoring just a few minutes after coming on as a substitute. The Nigeria striker wrong-footed Sean Steur with an impudent piece of skill before rolling the ball into the bottom corner.

The North-East club are coming to terms with the departures of Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães this summer, as well as manager Eddie Howe. They have one more pre-season friendly to play, against Strasbourg on Sunday, before they begin their Premier League campaign at home to Liverpool.

Newcastle United (4-2-3-1) Hornicek; M Miley (Pivas 81), Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Steur, L Miley (Finneran h-t); Elanga, Woltemade (Neave 86), Barnes; Wissa. Subs Charlton, Harris (g), Sanusi, Johnson.

Bayer Leverkusen (4-2-3-1) Flekken; Vazquez (Tape h-t), Bade, Tapsoba, Gutierrez (Belocian 70); Garcia, Fernandez (Terrier 70); Maza (Boniface 80), Tillman (Doganay 70), Moreira (Tella 80); Kofane (Schick h-t). Subs Hofmann, Arthur, Oermann, Poku, Blaswich (g), Alfa-Ruprecht, Hawighorst, Lomb (g).

Referee Michael Oliver (Durham). Attendance 39,059

A second pre-season defeat in a week for Newcastle. Just like against Everton, they faded in the second 45 minutes but Jaissle decided to leave some tired legs out there for fitness purposes. The performances of Barnes and Wissa were promising, but Newcaslte are giving up chances.

Newcastle had a free-kick with the last kick of the game, but Harvey Barnes loops the delivery straight into Flekken’s gloves.

Schik with a chance to wrap up the victory, but Hornicek saves before Thiaw clears to deny Terrier a tap in on the rebounds.

There will be just three minutes of added time to play.

Elanga fouled near the touchline, but time is running out. The free-kick won by Neave came to nothing.

Chance for Barnes! Good combination play involving Elanga and Wissa down the right, and the ball flashed across the six-yard box. Barnes almost steered it in, but did not make firm enough contact.

Newcastle attacking with more urgency since conceding, but there are moans and groans in the ground at a misplaced Elanga pass. Sean Neave has just replaced Woltemade, and the 19-year-old wins a free-kick in a crossing position with his first action of the game.

The striker has only been on the pitch a few minutes, but Boniface has restored Leverkusen’s lead. Lovely chop inside the box, which sent Steur for a hot dog, before passing the ball into the far corner. No celebration of note from a player who could be on the move this summer.

Newcastle making just their second change of the game: Pivas replaces Mason Miley at right-back.

Leverkusen have made two more changes: Moreira and Maza off, Tella and Boniface on.

The corner is straight down the throat of Flekken, and that prompsts some groans from the home fans.

Newcastle having to defend deep for long periods, but Elanga did well to win a free-kick with little support. Moreira dragged the winger down. Then Wissa’s cross is turned behind for a corner.

Woltemade’s control lets him down as he tries to bring the ball down on halfway. The game is being played at a snail’s pace at the moment, but Leverkusen are dominating the ball.

Play has now resumed. Garcia does well to defend after Lewis Hall won the ball back in a dangerous position.

Time for another hydration break and Leverkusen are making three more substitutions. We await further changes from Jaissle. Should the game finish level, there will be a penalty shoot-out to decide the winner of the Visit Malta Cup.

Rather like the mid-week friendly against Everton, Newcastle have faded after half-time. Struggling to get into the game in any meaningful way. Slick football from Leverkusen but Fernandez fails to bring the ball under his spell in the box when there was time and space to shoot.

Leverkusen just inches away from regaining the lead. It was an incisive run off the left from Afonso Moreira, who tried to place the ball into the far corner but his attempt rolled just wide of the post.

Good defensive header by Lewis Hall before Wissa wins a foul on halfway. Newcastle feeding off scraps at the moment. Elanga goes too early and is flagged offside.

Bayer Leverkusen have had the better of it in this half, but some of the shooting has been wayward. This time is it Schik’s turn to slash a shot over the bar. Fouls committed by Finneran and Botman.

Newcastle with a three-on-three on the break after Wissa does well to win the ball back on halfway, but Woltemade was too slow to get his shot away at the end of the move. More good play from Wissa.

Half a chance for Fernandez to shoot from the edge of the D, but he was leaning back and ballooned the shot miles over the bar.

Finneran, the youngster in Newcastle’s midfield, is caught on the ball but then does well to recover it. I reckon there will be a raft of changes on the hour mark.

Corner for Leverkusen after Moreira gets forward and attacks Mason Miley. The German side have additional aerial threat with Schik on the pitch. Woltemade does well to head clear.

Bayer Leverkuen kick off in the second half.

Jaissle made 10 against Everton, so wants his starters to build minutes today. Rory Finneran is coming on for Newcastle, an 18-year-old academy player. He replaces Lewis Miley in midfield. Czech striker Patrik Schik is on for Bayer Leverkusen.

The scoreline is a fair reflection of an even first half, with Wissa Newcastle’s best player. The story though, is that kit clash that prompted Newcastle to change into their lilac third kit halfway through the half.

Just the two minutes of stoppage time to play.

Newcastle equalise from a set-piece. Flekken is claiming a foul, but it is a legitimate goal. The goalkeeper was nowhere to be seen on a corner that looped all the way to be back post, and he seemed to lose his bearings allowing Thiaw to find the far corner.

Newcastle have a corner after another move in which Wissa was lively. His performances have been a ray of light in pre-season, he really struggled in his first season at the club.

Lewis Hall takes the free-kick, but he scoops it well over the bar. Elanga delivers a low cross from the right, but Garcia is well positioned to clear.

Newcastle enjoying a lot more possession now, but you cannot say they look like equalising.

That was better though, more zip in the attack with Elanga laying the ball off for Wissa and Fernandez is booked from dragging the Newcastle forward to the ground. Free-kick in a shooting position.

Good play from Lewis Hall, skipping beyond two challenges to escape from a tight spot but then his crossfield pass is intercepted. Moreira passes the ball straight out of play for a Newcastle goal kick, when there was a chance for Leverkusen to punish the hosts on the break.

Elanga tries to take on Gutierrez but his low cross is too close to Flekken. Gutierrez then buys a foul when under pressure from Lewis Miley. Game has become quite bitty following those stoppages. Maza then chops down Harvery Barnes.

The game is back under way. Changing kits has improved things visually but it is still not ideal. You wonder how on earth two clubs of this stature failed to liaise on this before the game.

Bayer Leverkusen are still on top, but play has been stopped for a hydration break. Some boos from the stands, it is not an especially hot day.

On the subject of the kit clash, Newcastle are now changing into their lilac away kit. Shades of Manchester United at the Dell all those years ago.

A short stoppage in play after Tapsoba receives a knock in the small of the back from Newcastle’s goalkeeper Hornicek. Both managers get their players over for a tactical conflab.

Leverkusen look very accomplished in possession, they are moving the ball well through the lines. Kofane was a big threat when they played Arsenal in last season’s Champions League and they are looking to find him with crosses. Mason Miley defends well at right-back, but at the expense of a corner.

Flekken called into action again, Newcastle starting to warm to their task. It was direct play from first Elanga and then Barnes, but his cross deflects towards the goalkeeper and he parries away. Then Barnes is fouled, and Newcastle have a free-kick in a crossing position near the left corner of the penalty area. Poor delivery from Barnes, Flekken claims.

Newcastle fans sing “walking in a Keegan wonderland” in unison. Bade is then penalised for catching Woltemade late as they contested an aerial challenge.

Newcastle’s best moment so far: Wissa peels off the shoulder of Bade and tested Flekken with a volley from a tight angle. The goalkeeper saved and Leverkusen scramble clear, but it was good movement from the Newcastle striker.

Leverkusen continue to make the running, enjoying more possession and most of it is coming inside Newcastle’s half. Goalkeeper Flekken takes a beat inside his own six-yard box, and his pass out is almost cut out by Woltemade.

Newcastle’s players are wearing black armbands in memory of Kevin Keegan.

There is a slightly awkward clash of kits on display: both shirts feature a lot of white, and the blue trim around the shoulders of Newcastle’s home kit is quite similar to Leverkusen’s away strip.

Kofane, who impressed up front last season in Germany, throws himself at a cross.

Fans were barely settled in their seats when Maza’s vicious left-footed strike from outside of the area flew past Hornicek. Cracking goal, not much the goalkeeper could do about it.

Matthias Jaissle walks to the home dugout for the first time as manager. Just eight days until the proper stuff begins against Liverpool, a fixture which tends to throw up entertaining games. Bayer Leverkusen keep the home players waiting in the tunnel.

The former Liverpool defender has been linked with a move to Arsenal this week. Quansah is with his team-mates but not part of the matchday squad.

Bayer Leverkusen XI: Flekken; Gutierrez, Bade, Fernandez, Moreira, Tillman, Tapsoba, Arthur, Garcia, Maza, Kofane

Subs: Blaswich, Lomb, Hofmann, Terrier, Schick, Oermann, Tape, Poku, Vazquez, Boniface, Tella, Alfa-Ruprecht, Doganay, Hawighorst

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; M Miley, Thiaw (c), Botman, Hall; Steur, L Miley; Elanga, Woltemade, Barnes; Wissa

Subs: Harris, Charlton, Pivas, Sanusi, Johnson, Finneran, Neave

Today's team to take on Bayer Leverkusen in the @VisitMalta Weekender 👊 pic.twitter.com/ZfRvucBXSq

Newcastle United continue their preparations for the new season with a home friendly against Bayer Leverkusen, hoping to improve on their pretty limp showing against Everton at Murrayfield.

New manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the Premier League season, insisting that he sees opportunity in the situation. Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who had lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

#1789. Man United transfer news: Major new rival emerges in race for Alejandro Balde

By Axel Clody | 18 Nov 2026 10:15

Lacking game time at Barcelona, Alejandro Balde is looking for a way out in January, with Paris Saint-Germain only just appearing in the picture.

Alejandro Balde is set to be one of the talking points of the winter transfer window. Struggling at Barcelona, where his game time has fallen considerably, the 23-year-old left-back is considering leaving to find a bigger role elsewhere.

His record this season is particularly meagre, with five appearances and only 124 minutes played. It is a situation that contrasts sharply with the status the Spaniard enjoyed in Catalonia until very recently.

According to the latest information from Spain and Italy, several clubs are following his situation. Juventus are considering a loan, while Monaco are eyeing a bigger move. Now Paris Saint-Germain and Manchester United have also entered the fray.

Manchester United are reportedly going all out to sign Balde in January.

According to TEAMtalk, the club’s recruitment department believes the left-back has a high ceiling and Barcelona are open to a loan, which would allow Manchester United to assess him before committing to a permanent deal.

The same report says Balde is willing to move to the Premier League and that his relationship with Barcelona manager Hansi Flick is ‘completely broken and glacial’.

Fabrizio Romano has described the chance of a January exit as ‘serious and concrete’, adding that Balde is ‘genuinely ready to consider leaving’ and exploring options with his agent, Jorge Mendes. Manchester United were interested in the summer but did not proceed, with Balde considered too expensive for a left-back, in talks said to have involved a fee of €50m-€55m (£42.5m-£46.5m) and a net salary of more than €5m (£4.3m).

Valued at around €40m (£34m), the Barcelona player represents a market opportunity for Paris Saint-Germain. At 23, Balde already has significant experience at the highest level and still has room for improvement.

Quick and explosive, he fits the profile of a modern full-back and offers better guarantees than Lucas Digne, the disappointing summer signing. His ability to get in behind and create overloads would give Luis Enrique’s team another attacking dimension, and the move could also be a fresh start for a player who has lost confidence and continuity at Barcelona, not least because Luis Enrique rotates his starting line-up heavily.

The main obstacle is Nuno Mendes, who owns the left-back position at Paris Saint-Germain and is one of the best players in the world in that role, if not the best.

At 24, the Portuguese is a major part of the club’s project, and the left-footed Balde cannot play on the right side of defence, unless the manager comes up with something.

Luis Enrique also generally prefers a right-footed winger on the left, so Paris Saint-Germain could sign an excellent player without offering him a lasting prospect of starting, with a real risk of frustration.

#1784. Chelsea: Mykhailo Mudryk points finger for drugs ban as Tottenham loan star prepares for comeback

Your weekly briefing on Chelsea, featuring team news and expert analysis from Dom Smith

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed the Ukrainian football association for his doping ban.

The Chelsea winger, currently on loan at Tottenham, sat out the entirety of the 2025-26 season due to a positive drugs test for meldonium, a banned substance, back in October 2024.

The substance is believed to enhance stamina and respiratory capacity.

The forward was allowed to play once more in the summer, when his four-year ban, that he appealed through the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), was lifted.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso pushed for the winger to go out on loan to earn regular game time, and he reunited with his former boss at Shakhtar Donetsk, Roberto De Zerbi, at Spurs.

Now, Mudryk has pointed the finger at the Ukrainian FA for the ‘adverse finding’ in his out-of-competition sample that was supplied two years ago.

"It was a bolt from the blue,” he said of his positive drugs test on Ukrainian podcast ‘Guest of Gordon’.

“I couldn’t believe it was true. It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on failing. It hit me very hard, mentally.”

The 25-year-old claims that he had never heard of meldonium, insisting that there was “no security” on international duty.

“It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe,” he explained. “It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.”

Asked how it had got into his system, he replied: "The Ukrainian national team has absolutely no security system. At clubs, when you travel to an away game, there are always people responsible for what happens on the hotel floors and in the team.

“There are people who keep an eye on it. In the Ukrainian national team we have a nutritionist who hands us pills every couple of days before games.

“He brings us a little cup. Everyone has to take the pills that are in that cup.”

The winger, who moved to Stamford Bridge in 2023 for an initial £62million - that could rise to £89m - was asked point-blank if he blamed his national setup.

He is hoped to be back this weekend for Spurs’ home game against Ipswich.

#1778. Max Dowman breaks Jude Bellingham record: what makes the Arsenal gem so special?

By Axel Clody | 18 Nov 2026 11:31

Max Dowman, who turns 17 soon, has already made history in the Premier League, the Champions League and for England

It seems that every piece of news about Max Dowman starts the same way: the young Arsenal player has broken another record. At 16, the Englishman has already been the youngest player to score in the Premier League, to play in the Champions League and to win the English league title.

This week, he added two more marks to the list: he became the youngest player to represent the England Under-21s and, three days later, the youngest to score for the side, surpassing records that belonged to Jude Bellingham.

The question is not only how many more records he can break, but what makes Dowman such a special talent and how far his characteristics can take him. The combination of individual skill, ball carrying, strength to compete physically and understanding of the game helps to explain why he can already produce against much older opponents.

Dowman was born on 31 December 2009 and joined Arsenal as a child. His progress through the youth ranks was so rapid that, at 13, he was already playing for the Under-18s. In September 2024, aged 14 years and eight months, he made his debut in the UEFA Youth League, an Under-19 competition, and became the youngest scorer in the history of the tournament.

The midfielder began training with the first team at 14 and took part in the 2025 pre-season. In August of that year, aged 15 years and 235 days, he made his Premier League debut against Leeds United. He was the second-youngest player to appear in the competition’s history, behind only Ethan Nwaneri, his Arsenal team-mate.

In November 2025, an even more significant milestone arrived. Coming on in the 3-0 win over Slavia Prague in the Champions League, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the tournament’s history, aged 15 years and 308 days. He was also the first 15-year-old to play in the competition.

The 2025-26 season brought two more high-profile records. In March, he scored against Everton and, aged 16 years and 73 days, became the youngest scorer in Premier League history, beating James Vaughan’s mark by 197 days.

Months later, he went down in Arsenal history as the youngest player to win the Premier League. The medal came at 16 years and 144 days, when the club ended a 22-year wait for the title. In October, he received three Guinness World Records certificates for the achievements.

Now, the England Under-21s have added two more chapters. Dowman made his debut for the side against Portugal on 13 November, aged 16 years and 317 days, surpassing Bellingham’s mark as the youngest player to represent the age group. On the following Monday, he started for the first time and scored the winning goal against France, aged 16 years and 320 days. Bellingham had scored his first Under-21 goal aged 17 years and 67 days.

Records broken for Arsenal and England (born 31/12/2009)

If he scores for the senior England team before 12/11/2027, Dowman will surpass Wayne Rooney (17 years and 317 days, in 2003) as the youngest scorer for England.

Age in years (y) and days (d) on the date of each record. n/a = previous holder not confirmed by an official source. Data up to 17/11/2026.

Sources: Arsenal, Premier League, ESPN and TNT Sports

Dowman’s main characteristic is his ability to carry the ball and beat opponents. He finds it easy to receive under pressure, shield possession with his body and change direction in tight spaces. He does not rely on straight-line speed alone: he uses feints, changes of pace and short movements to unbalance defenders.

Dowman already had a physique that allowed him to compete with older players, but he has also developed an intelligent way of using his body to protect the ball. That explains why he does not seem so intimidated when facing professional defenders.

Left-footed, he usually plays on the right, from where he can cut inside and use his dominant foot. The position also allows him to receive wide, draw the opposing full-back and choose between accelerating towards the box, combining with a team-mate or finding a pass inside. His ball control and ability to change the direction of play make him a particularly difficult threat to handle one-on-one.

But reducing him to a dribbling winger would ignore an important part of his repertoire. Dowman also has experience playing as an attacking midfielder and in deeper roles. In the youth ranks, he even played as a deep-lying midfielder. This variety helped him develop a broader understanding of space and the different roles on the pitch.

That versatility is an advantage for Arteta. At Arsenal, Dowman has already been used on the right and in central positions. When he receives between the lines, he can turn quickly and carry the ball towards the opposition defence. If he starts wide, he can attack the space between full-back and centre-back, moving closer to the box to shoot or take part in a combination.

There are also signs that his play without the ball matches his technical quality. In the win over France, Lee Carsley highlighted the teenager’s defensive performance, as he dropped back to intercept a pass and joined the pressing of opponents. A willingness to recover, press and take part in collective actions is an important requirement for earning a place in a side like Arteta’s.

Dowman’s rise inevitably prompts comparisons. His path recalls, in some respects, that of Nwaneri, who also made his Arsenal debut very young and had to find space in a competitive squad. Both came through the youth ranks playing in central positions, but had their first opportunities in the first team on the right.

The difference is that Dowman seems to have an even clearer ability to carry the ball at speed and beat opponents one-on-one. That does not mean it is possible to determine who will have the more successful career.

Arsenal also have reason to manage expectations. The recent episode against Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup highlighted one area of concern. After suffering a heavy challenge, the teenager reacted and was sent off, receiving a three-match ban. Arteta criticised the player publicly and said professional football is not an environment protected from provocation and the consequences of one’s own actions.

There is also the question of workload. A player who starts playing professional matches so early needs physical and emotional support. Arsenal have recent experience of integrating young players such as Saka, Nwaneri and Lewis-Skelly, but each athlete has his own process.

His first professional contract will be signed when he turns 17 on 31 December, after he agreed a pre-contract with Arsenal in January. The decision to stay at the club is important for the continuity of a development that has been closely monitored since the youth ranks.

The path to the senior England team is also open, but does not need to be taken immediately. Bellingham, who lost the Under-21 records to Dowman, played only four matches at that level before being promoted to the senior team.

For now, the best way to assess Dowman is to look at what he can already do, without turning every record into a career prediction. The rest depends on development, opportunities and careful management.
