#1732. Same old Spurs given reality check of epic proportions

The players and the transfer fees might be different, but this was same old Tottenham Hotspur. The same Tottenham that finished each of the last two seasons in 17th. The same Tottenham that folded in adversity. The same Tottenham that opposition fans loved to laugh at.

Of course, it is very early days and the good news for Spurs fans and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is the side that started the opening day humiliation to Brentford may well never play together again this season.

But in a summer in which Tottenham have allowed their fans to dream of good times ahead by breaking the bank in the transfer window, this was a reality check of epic proportions.

The Spurs supporters who have become sick of being made the butt of their rivals’ jokes had to listen to Brentford fans singing “Thomas Frank, he’s laughing at you” in reference to the Dane’s unhappy spell in north London.

The impending arrival of Savinho will take Tottenham’s spending over £300m, but none of their big-money debutants at the Gtech Community Stadium hit the ground running.

There was only one man who looked anything close to a £100m player and it was not Sandro Tonali.

Tottenham’s first-ever £100m signing was completely upstaged by Brentford’s Mamadou Sangaré on his first competitive start for the club, as Spurs were run ragged.

Sangaré might not have scored on his Brentford debut, but he had a major contribution in two of his side’s goals and bossed the middle of the park. He deservedly received a standing ovation when he was substituted with 15 minutes remaining.

“He is a top player, no doubt about it,” said head coach Keith Andrews. “He is the one we were after in the window. The club deserve a lot of credit because a lot of clubs were looking at him.

“He deserves a lot of credit too, because he could have gone elsewhere for a few more bob. He recognised this would be a good place to come and he has settled quite nicely.”

A club-record £39m signing from French club Lens, Sangaré may prove to be a steal for Brentford. He ran the game for long periods and was responsible for Keane Lewis-Potter’s opening goal.

Having played a lovely one-two with Dango Ouattara, Sangaré kept his cool to brilliantly pick out Lewis-Potter and give him the easy task of finding the back of the net.

Keane Lewis-Potter scores Brentford's first goal of the new season!Brilliant play from record signing Mamadou Sangaré 👏 pic.twitter.com/Ua9HklQaWh

Later in the first half, Sangaré won a free-kick in his own half thanks to some quick feet and the action produced a big cheer from the home fans.

Tonali was the subject of chants of “what a waste of money” from Brentford supporters. It was a volley that sailed high over the crossbar that prompted that particular song, but Tonali was not just off target with his shooting.

He lost possession on a couple of occasions at both ends of the pitch and allowed Brentford players to glide past him during the opening stages of the match. He struggled to get around the pitch and Tottenham generally lacked desire and fight – two things that clubs cannot buy.

Richarlison, Lucas Bergvall and goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky can all be disappointed with Brentford’s second goal. Richarlison’s hold-up play was terrible, Bergvall produced a weak challenge that allowed Mathias Jensen to take the ball and shoot, and Kinsky parried the ball straight into the path of Vitaly Janelt, who scored.

Kinsky has been trusted to take over from Guglielmo Vicario as Tottenham’s number one this season, but this was not a good start.

Vitaly Janelt doubles Brentford's lead! 🐝 pic.twitter.com/AYh5BGhJBQ

De Zerbi spent much of the first half telling his back four to get higher up the pitch and it was perhaps understandable that captain for the day Archie Gray, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson looked like a group of strangers.

This was the foursome’s first competitive game together, but De Zerbi will need his Tottenham players to get to know each other as fast as possible if they are to challenge for Europe this season or even finish in the top half of the table.

Bergvall and Conor Gallagher were hooked at half-time, with Tottenham two goals behind and De Zerbi clearly unimpressed. But the Italian’s changes did not prompt an instant response. In fact, things got even worse.

Once again, Sangaré was heavily involved. He produced a well-hit shot that Kinsky had to save. For the second time, the goalkeeper failed to push the ball out of trouble and Michael Kayode was able to score.

Michael Kayode with a third for Brentford just three minutes into the second half! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/40kOIlV5MU

Igor Thiago missed a penalty after substitute Rodrigo Bentancur fouled Kevin Schade, as Spurs threatened to completely collapse with the result already pretty much decided.

Igor Thiago's penalty CRASHES off the post! ❌ pic.twitter.com/jZUEoIA44h

De Zerbi can console himself with the fact his Spurs team will quickly look a lot different. There are more new faces to come in, with winger Savinho on the brink of joining and Tottenham hoping Omar Marmoush will follow him from Manchester City.

Mikey Moore, who forced Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher into two second-half saves, is expected to join Cologne on loan and Mohammed Kudus is close to returning from injury, while Micky van de Ven and Pedro Porro will come back in.

But if ever there was proof that spending a fortune offers no guarantee of happiness, then this was it.

Roberto De Zerbi has admitted that big-spending Tottenham Hotspur “are not a team yet” after watching his new-look side fall to an opening-day defeat to Brentford.

Tottenham have splashed out over £200m on new players, but head coach De Zerbi has warned it will be impossible to set any targets until they become a team.

Record £100m signing Sandro Tonali made his competitive debut for Tottenham, along with fellow new signings Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi, Mateus Fernandes and Andy Robertson.

Tottenham have been tipped to challenge for European qualification, having finished 17th in each of the last two seasons, but De Zerbi acknowledged those optimistic predictions may have come too soon.

His team looked like strangers in their humiliating loss at Brentford and the Italian said: “We are not a team yet for a lot of reasons. We can fix the target [for the season] when you become a team. Before you become a team, you can’t say what you can do.

“You can’t become a team from the transfer market on paper. You become a team when the players find a connection, a spirit, a soul.

“We are not at the right point in our physical condition for a lot of reasons. Late from the World Cup and because in Australia [on pre-season], we don’t work in the right way. But no excuses, it’s a normal situation when you are building a new project. I don’t want time but we have to pass through these problems.

“I am surprised by the result and performance. They [Brentford] deserved to win and we played very bad. I knew we were not in the right condition. We can’t find an excuse. I am sorry for the result and performance.

“Marcos Senesi, Jan Paul van Hecke and Sandro Tonali are not in the best physical condition. We knew that before the game. We have to improve on that and many other things, like organisation and pressing.

“We can improve quickly but first, we have to understand this game better. I know their physical condition and [they are] new players but we have to put something more.

“We had to fight more. Players know I have a lot of confidence in them and we hope to improve quickly. Until we reach these conditions we have to suffer and today is an important defeat. Maybe we can wake up stronger.”

We had some problems with the timing of the pressure, we arrived too often late. We lost too many duels to compete with Brentford. I am sorry for that and sorry for the defeat. We have to improve in the physical condition and the organisation.

It was the first game and part of our journey, we knew we had a lot of new players. To become a team I said before the game we need two things, soul and style of play. We didn’t fight in the right way. Brentford is maybe one of the most important teams in the Premier League in terms of duels.

It was a game, especially in the first half, in one direction. We were not in the right position to make the high pressure, with Mikey Moore on the left centre.

We didn’t play well, we didn’t play in the right way. I think not because we don’t remember last season, because these players are good people but we lost too many duels. One of the best qualities of Brentford is the one-to-one, the man-to-man and the set-pieces.

Really pleased. Felt like there was a performance coming, you never really know after pre-season. The reality is the first game of the season comes and it can quickly come unstuck. I felt good for a number of weeks about how we were coming together. I was pretty pleased.

Our fans were amazing today. There is a genuine connection here that helps. I thought we started the game brilliantly and they were fully engaged. We want to be relentless. We looked like a real team.

That’s what we wanted, we wanted to start sharp, we want to show people what we’re made of and we did that today. We know last season we were one point off, this year, we’ve added quality people to the squad.

He’s been unbelievable, I can’t praise him high enough. He’s one of them players that we might lose the ball you just know he is going to win it back and he gets us on the counter-attack so quickly.

Is that Pedro Porro, Micky Van de Ven and Mohammed Kudus could be back for the next game against Newcastle, and Savinho ought to be through the door.

According to Opta, Brentford won the xG battle 3.96 to 0.47, taking 26 shots to Spurs’s nine. De Zerbi’s team finished the game with 59 per cent possession, but that is inflated by Brentford sitting off when three up. It’s the most xG Spurs have conceded in a single game since a 6-3 defeat by Liverpool in December 2024.

Less Christ the Redeemer more Christ, that was terrible.

"I think that sums it up"Fair to say this Spurs fan wasn't pleased with their performance 😅 pic.twitter.com/ZAdVaVbjlS

Possibly Brentford’s best performance under Keith Andrews, though that may be overstating the strength of the opposition. This was a complete display: they pressed Spurs, they played through Spurs, they played over Spurs, they dominated Spurs from set-pieces and their defenders bullied Spurs’s forwards. It will be interesting to hear from De Zerbi and whether he is philosophical or irate. This is far from Spurs’s ideal projected team, but still unacceptable.

Kinsky palms away a Damsgaard corner, and Yarmoliuk slices his shot over the bar. We are deep into stoppage time, and Brentford’s players are still pressing Bentnacur and Senesi and making them play with their heads down.

Just four minutes of added time to play but Spurs have more defending to do in the shape over another Brentford corner. They survive, but Brentford quickly establish possession again.

It would appear Lord Sugar is still watching:

To all Spurs fans don't worry this is all tactical to lure other teams into believing we are a easy touch. #coys

Another Brentford debut: Callum Wilson replaces Igor Thiago. Destiny Udogie has replaced Archie Gray for Spurs. “You should have signed for a big club!” sing the Brentford fans, in reference to the club almost signing Gray two summers ago. Football fans never forget.

Another Brentford goal would put them top of the table, for what that is worth. Spurs enjoying some possession in the Brentford half now, but it is entirely sterile.

Igor Thiago’s shot is blocked, Brentford still look the more likely team to score the next goal. Jadon Anthony shows he has a long throw, which might be a small reason why Brentford decided to sign him. Janelt then drags back Maddison.

Jadon Anthony involved in some Brenford pressure that results in a long throw and a corner, but the new man then slices a volley over the bar. Standing ovation at the Gtech for Sangare as he makes way for Damsgaard, while Hickey replaces Kayode. Be tough to beat his performance as debut of the weekend.

Michael Oliver letting some meaty challenges go, the game is quite feisty despite the scoreline. Schade launched himself into a tackle on Solanke but he did not really catch him with his studs.

A few Spurs fans may have thought better of staying to watch the final 20 minutes. I wonder “if” this Spurs fan has switched the television off?

First match if season . Smiling before the game. Hope to be smiling after. pic.twitter.com/hsTc79PBti

Richarlison beats the turf and Ajer punches the air after the Brentford defender wins the foul. Andrews is making another couple of changes: Jensen and Ouattara off, Yarmoliuk and new signing Jadon Anthony on.

Two more Spurs changes too: Maddison and Solanke on, Moore and Richarlison off.

Really sharp save from Kelleher to keep out Moore’s powerful shot from close range. Moore has at least carried a threat for Spurs in the second half, but they are struggling to sustain much pressure.

Tonali with a hit from 25 yards but it deflects comfortably into the arms of Kelleher. Surely a (Kew?) bridge too far for Spurs to dig out any kind of result from here.

De Zerbi looks a little resigned on the touchline, he will know that this is far from his ideal Spurs team on the pitch but that cannot excuse such poor standards.

He fails to open his account for the season. Sent Kinsky the wrong way, but he dragged the penalty just a touch and it cannoned off the post. The lead remains three.

Igor Thiago's penalty CRASHES off the post! ❌ pic.twitter.com/jZUEoIA44h

Spurs are being overpowered here, they cannot cope whenever Brentford come forward. There were appeals for handball against Van Hecke after Janelt swivelled and shot, but the foul is given against Bentancur for bundling over Schade. A complete mess for Spurs.

Any hope that the half-time double change would bring a revival now appear forlorn.

But here is a chance for Mikey Moore! Robertson forward to good effect, and his low cross arrives to Moore at the back post but his shot was too close to Kelleher. Almost crept through his legs.

Well that is surely game over. Cracking strike from Sangare from the edge of the box after a Brentford corner is cleared, they have always been so good at winning those second balls. Driven strike, good save from Kinsky and Kayode is first to the rebound to score from a couple of yards.

Michael Kayode with a third for Brentford just three minutes into the second half! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/40kOIlV5MU

Important defensive header from Van Hecke to repel Sangare’s dangerous cross, and we enjoy our first look at a Kayode long throw. Some Strictly Come Dancing moves from Senesi and Collins in the penalty area, and the referee has a word with them. It continues when the throw is taken, and Sensi has a chunk of his shirt, but VAR says the Spurs man was fouled beforehand.

Will we see a different Tottenham in the second half.

Gallagher and Bergvall hooked, replaced by Bentancur and Fernandes who makes his Spurs debut.

15 - There was 15 passes in the build-up to Keane Lewis-Potter's opening goal for Brentford, only Michael Kayode's goal v Wolves in March (19) and Rico Henry's goal v Bournemouth in December (18) have seen more in a Premier League goal for the Bees under Keith Andrews.Busy. pic.twitter.com/8j5RZWFxvH

This has been a dreadful start to the season by Tottenham. Sandro Tonali has barely looked like a £10m player, let alone a £100m midfielder and, maybe unsurprisingly, De Zerbi’s players look like strangers. He will demand a major improvement in the second half. Keith Andrews will be delighted - maybe other than the fact the game isn’t already dead. His team have been dominant.

Brentford utterly dominant, there has been an alarming gulf in industry, precision and class between the two teams. Spurs will surely improve, both in the second half and as the season goes on, but this has fallen well below the standards you expect of a team with European aspirations. If a few of these players never played for De Zerbi again they could have no complaints.

No sign of a Spurs revival at half time, Brentford playing through their press with ease and then have space to run into. Kayode wins his header at the back post but no player was there for the knockdown.

Important block from Ajer after Spurs’s best piece of combination play around the box, before Tonali slashes a volley well over the bar from distance. Cue “what a waste of money” from the home fans.

Richarlison has been non-existent up front for Spurs, bullied by Collins and Ajer.

Tonali with a stray midfield pass to Outtara which rather sums up the Spurs performance so far. Surely there will be sweeping changes from De Zerbi at half time. Solanke, Maddison and Fernandes are the three players you’d have in mind.

“You’re going down with the Fulham,” is the chant from the Brentford fans.

Lewis-Potter swings in a dangerous cross, headed down by Kayode, and Van Hecke stoops to block Outtara’s shot. The whistle goes for a high boot.

This is far from Spurs’s strongest hypothetical team but they are being taken to the cleaners here. Spurs caught in that Brentford man-to-man press again and the ball bounces off Richarlison. Jensen shoots with power from the edge of the box, and Kinsky bats the shot back into danger, and there was Janelt to poke the rebound home. Brentford in total control.

Vitaly Janelt doubles Brentford's lead! 🐝 pic.twitter.com/AYh5BGhJBQ

Spurs’s defence breached again, and Outtara really should have made it two but his first touch was far too heavy and Kinsky was able to clear. Spurs will not be the only team to struggle against this Brentford front three. Schade won the flick on, Thiago swept the ball across the box, but the finish was lacking from Outtara.

Outtara fouls his former Bournemouth team-mate in the Spurs box. A lovely chipped pass forward from Schade releases Thiago in the left channel and another spell of home pressure begins. Lewis-Potter roaming everywhere. Then Brentford win a free-kick which will go in the mixer. Senesi fouled Outtara.

Bergvall floats in a decent cross from the left but it splits Richarlison and Moore. Sweden manager Graham Potter is in the stands watching Bergvall. Van Hecke is known for his progressive passes, but he overhits one through for a Brentford goal kick.

Spurs players not happy with Michael Oliver. Conor Gallagher feels he was pulled back in midfield, before Oliver blows for a 50:50 in Brentford’s favour.

All so simple for Brentford to get at Spurs again, and it takes some excellent defending on the cover from Robertson to deny Outarra who could have been through for a second goal.

Igor Thiago’s header hits the bar but the flag goes up for offside. Brentford’s man-to-man press is smothering Spurs at the moment, they cannot break through it to establish any territory higher up the pitch.

Igor Thiago makes enough of a nuisance of himself to force Senesi to put the ball out for a throw, Brazil vs Argentina in the match up. Brentford just look sharper and more match-ready all over the pitch.

Half a chance for Spurs to reply with a quickfire equaliser, but Tel’s free-kick was tame and deflected through to Kelleher. De Zerbi can have no complaints, it was one-way traffic before the goal.

Well that’s a good early impression from Sangare. He played a lovely one-two before picking out Lewis-Potter for Brentford’s goal.

To say this opening Brentford goal was on the cards would be a mammoth understatement. The home team are finding it so easy to progress the ball to dangerous positions around the Spurs box.

The new man Sangare is involved, playing a one-two at the edge of the area, before picking out Lewis-Potter who was unmarked on the penalty spot. Brentford’s left back popping up in the box, and it is a simple finish.

Keane Lewis-Potter scores Brentford's first goal of the new season!Brilliant play from record signing Mamadou Sangaré 👏 pic.twitter.com/Ua9HklQaWh

Pretty much Spurs’s first meaningful foray over the halfway line, but Gallagher’s shot from distance is wild. In other news, Jon Bon Jovi is in the stands. He popped up at a few games at the World Cup.

Brentford continue to make inroads down their left, Lewis-Potter driving at Gray and whipping in a dangerous cross that glanced off Van Hecke at the near post and only just wide of the far post. The corner is swung to the unmarked Sangare at the back post, and his header loops well over.

Brentford continue to look the better team, moving the ball at pace in the final third, but Schade stumbles up against Bergvall in the box. Spurs yet to settle of establish any possession in the game so far.

Collins then catches Gallagher on the foot, as the Spurs man rushed into a challenge to close the defender down. Not much in it.

From that free-kick, Jenson’s delivery was a wicked one: inswinging and flat to the near post, and the ball glanced off Robertson’s head and behind for a corner.

Jensen then tees up Lewis-Potter for an ambitious volley from the edge of the box, and there are hopeful appeals for a handball penalty against Gallagher, and then Collins fails to divert to follow up cross on target.

Not the most distinctive contrast between the two kits, but not as bad as Newcastle vs Bayer Leverkusen in pre-season.

Brentford on the front foot in the early exchanges, Sangare involve in their first attack, but Tel runs back to defend well against Kayode.

Schade then wins a free-kick from Van Hecke in a crossing position wide left, the forward’s feet were too quick for the Dutch defender.

The usual rendition of Hey Jude before the game in south west London.

[On three of the back four being new signings] I have a big confidence because all three are very important players with experience and qualities. They have been working for one month and we have no problem with them.

[On Gray wearing the armband] He’s very young but he is a big personality. great behaviour and he deserves to be a captain today. He cannot suffer too much pressure because he is an important player for us for a long time.

[On if there is more business to be done] We have not the right or complete squad today but no excuse we have the qualities to compete against an important team with a clear style, they are very strong in set-pieces and long balls especially.

This will be a first look at new signing Mamadou Sangare for Brentford fans. Lots of people have tipped him to be one of the signings of the summer. I haven’t seen enough of him to give an opinion but it will be interesting to see how he gets on against Tottenham’s first-ever £100m man Sandro Tonali.

There’s a decent chance this Tottenham starting line-up will not play again together for the rest of this season. Mikey Moore is expected to move to Cologne on loan, while Savinho’s arrival will relegate Mathys Tel to the bench. Spurs also have Mohamed Kudus and Xavi Simons to return from injury. De Zerbi will want a good start to the season, but this is not the Tottenham side he will be relying upon moving forwards.

There will be no easing into life at Spurs for Robertson, who faces Dango Outtara in one of the game’s key duels. The Scot has plenty of experience of course, but there were signs towards the end of time at Liverpool that he had started to struggle in one-on-ones against wingers.

Archie Gray will become Tottenham’s youngest-ever captain tonight. Aged 20 years and 163 days, he will beat Steve Perryman’s record of 20 years and 260 days. On Friday, De Zerbi listed all of his captains with Gray down in fifth place. New permanent captain Micky van de Ven misses the trip to Brentford through injury.

If we include the league goals Mikey Moore scored while on loan at Rangers last season, Spurs’s front three scored 22 league goals combined last season. By contrast, Igor Thiago, Kevin Schade and Dango Outtara scored 37 between them in the Premier League. Brentford are firm favourites with the bookies for this one, and that difference in firepower is probably why. Omar Marmoush could help matters.

Seventeen-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett is one of the outstanding players in the country at his age group, and there is a lot of excitement about him at Spurs. Post-Kane, the club’s academy has not delivered much bona fide first-team quality, but Williams-Barnett appears on that trajectory.

Spurs XI: Kinsky; Gray, Van Hecke, Senesi, Robertson; Gallagher, Tonali, Bergvall; Moore, Richarlison, Tel

Subs: Dubravka, Danso, Maddison, Udogie, Fernandes, Solanke, Bentancur, Davies, Williams-Barnett

Our Spurs side on the opening day 🤍🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/Uh5z221aTc

Starting the season in west London 📌 pic.twitter.com/uglTu9zDvA

Former managers Mauricio Pochettino, José Mourinho, Antonio Conte and Ange Postecoglou will all be scratching their heads about Spurs’ change of strategy in the club’s first post-Levy summer.

It was Postecoglou who publicly shared his belief that Spurs would never spend £100m on a player and yet, just over a year after his departure, the club splashed out exactly that on midfielder Tonali.

Whereas Postecoglou and his predecessors often had to answer questions over Spurs’ perceived profligacy, De Zerbi has been able to tease fans with promises of “bomba” signings.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Brentford vs Tottenham Hotspur in the Premier League, a London derby between the smart spenders and the big spenders.

That is probably an unfair dichotomy, because Spurs’s squad has been crying out for investment, and that has certainly arrived this summer. The club’s new leadership team has overseen more than £300m worth of purchases.

The arrival of Jean Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi, two of the league’s best progressive passers from centre-back, makes it clear that improving Spurs’s build up play is a priority for Roberto De Zerbi.

De Zerbi wants his teams to draw pressure from opponents and progress down the middle of the pitch with short passes, so it was imperative that Spurs upgraded in midfield. They have done just that by buying Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali, for a combined £185m.

Spurs’s forward options remain much the same though, which could prove a drag in the season’s early weeks. Compared to Manchester United, Chelsea, and Liverpool, Spurs do not have the same firepower, but they should have more control and solidity this season.

Brentford lost just three league games at home last season, and they were unfortunate not to qualify for Europe. A lighter workload offers Keith Andrews the chance to consolidate on an excellent first season as head coach, and perhaps overtake some of those clubs with continental commitments.

Midfielder Mamadou Sangaré, signed for £39m from Lens, looks the pick of their summer business, tipped to be a £100m sale to one of the big boys (which is an unromantic perspective on the transfer, but very much Brentford’s model).

Asked about the Mali international, Andrews said: “He’s a very talented midfielder who can do lots of different aspects of that role.

“He’s a very focused, very determined and very ambitious young man. He’s very humble but equally as hungry to achieve impressive things. He’s certainly a player on an upward trajectory.”

Forwards Jadon Anthony and Callum Wilson are other arrivals, and Michael Kayode’s long throws will continue to be a serious weapon.

#1729. Is the Gyokeres iron hot enough for Hull?

I’m here for our book launch which takes place tonight, but also for our game against Hull tomorrow. Mikel Arteta will meet the press this afternoon ahead of that one, and we’ll bring you all the stories on Arseblog News. I don’t think there’s gonna be anything mind-blowing, it looked like we came through the Slavia Prague game without any issues, so fingers crossed that’s the case.

I suppose I’m mildly curious as to whether Viktor Gyokeres’ performance on Wednesday will see him keep his place up front. He got a great goal, provided an assist for Noni Madueke, and probably should have had another assist when he headed back across goal for Mikel Merino, only for the Spaniard to head over the bar when we know he can do better from those situations.

He’s a player who seems to need confidence and rhythm, and on that basis it would make some sense to keep him in the starting line-up. After the last Interlull, when he scored in four successive games for Sweden, I made the case that giving him a start in our first game back would make some sense to try and harness some of what was a good goal scoring run. Strike while the iron is hot and all that.

I looked at a home game against Leeds as the kind of fixture that would suit him. He scored two against them at home last season, and one at Elland Road, but when the time came Mikel Arteta picked Kai Havertz up front. Speaking about the decision to start Gyokeres on Wednesday in Prague, the manager said:

It was a game we believed would be really good for him, for the demands the opponent puts in and the spaces he could use. He’s done it really well, not just for the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s really great news for him, because he really needed that performance.

The question will be does Arteta think Hull at home will be as good for him as Slavia Prague away? After a bright start to the season they haven’t won any of their last seven but they have drawn five of those. Chances are they’re going to come and sit deep, using the blueprint we’ve seen many teams deploy against Arsenal in the past. If a Gyokeres game, if we can call it that, requires the opposition to leave spaces he can use (as per Arteta’s quote above), then maybe this isn’t one of those.

However, on paper, and with all due respect to tomorrow’s opposition, if Hull at home isn’t a Gyokeres game, then it’s hard not to be a bit worried. Personally, I’d be all right to see him start this one, and if it doesn’t work then you have other options. Havertz is the obvious one, but Mikel Merino is an alternative as well with his ability to find spaces inside the opponent’s penalty area. Ideally though, it’s a bit of a building block of a game for the Swedish international. We need him to deliver goals and assists, the last few weeks have been a bit more positive in that regard, and ultimately it’s important that the manager recognises the moments in a season when he might have to choose one player over another for the overall benefit of the team.

Which is to say, I look forward very much to seeing Declan Rice starting up front against Hull tomorrow, and Arteta revealing that his tech-boffins have invented a gizmo which will allow Rice to player 180 minutes in every game. Plus injury time. I kid, obviously, but I suppose we should know by now that regardless of what we think about team selections, use of players, and everything else, this manager will never be even remotely swayed by external noise – and that’s a good thing most of the time!

We will talk a bit more about the Hull game in a quick preview podcast on Patreon a little later on. Because of the book launch, we’ll be recording before the manager meets the press, so bear that in mind.

Hopefully catch lots of you later on at Big Red – and here’s a nice piece on the photos in the book. Just a reminder again that those who have registered to come to the launch, you can purchase the book via the email sent to you (check your junk folders if you don’t see it), so you can simply come and collect on the night. We can also facilitate sales via credit card etc if you don’t want to do that.

If you purchased via the Patreon pre-sale, those books are not for collection tomorrow, and will be shipped to you in due course. There is also some scope to come along on spec on the night, and we should have copies available but obviously priority goes to those who registered. We will then have a final batch of books going on general sale online on Saturday evening after the Hull game. Full details of that to follow here on site and via Arseblog on BlueSky.

#1728. Are you ok, Noni?

Arsenal’s squad construction has given them a lot of depth and diversity in terms of profiles. Timber and White for right-back, Calafiori and Hincapie for left-back. Ezri Konsa has, incredibly, offered both protection and threat to the impregnable Saliba and Gabriel partnership. Bruno and Lewis Skelly, Rice and Zubimendi and Odegaard and Merino for midfield.

Eze and Tzolis for the left-wing. Havertz and Gyokeres for centre-forward. Of course, some of these pairings are more symbiotic than others. Mosquera is probably going to fall behind Konsa as a back up to either one of Saliba or Gabriel. In reality, Zubimendi is only going to play ahead of Rice if Rice is injured or Arsenal have a nice easy game against League Two opposition, for example…

On the face of it, Noni Madueke should really be in that third layer of the squad with Mosquera, Kepa and where Zubimendi probably now resides. The role of back-up to Bukayo Saka ought to have been one with limited opportunity. In a sense, I was always a little surprised that Madueke signed up for it when he came to the club from Chelsea last summer.

I was slightly surprised that Arsenal spent so much money on a player who was always incredibly unlikely to dislodge Saka no matter how much he improved. And how much scope was there going to be for Madueke to get the sort of rhythm and consistency of selection to hone his talents?

Now I strongly suspect that Arsenal would have had anxieties over Saka’s ability to stay fit after tearing his hamstring in December 2024 and missing a few months of football. It was the first significant injury Saka had incurred and after quickly deciding that loanee winger Raheem Sterling was not going to be an adequate replacement, they amended for his absence with a blend of 17-year-old Ethan Nwaneri and surplus left-back Kieran Tierney.

It isn’t difficult to see how Arsenal viewed the right-wing spot as a single point of failure but encouraging Madueke to see it as an attractive position must have challenged even Mikel Arteta’s powers of persuasion. Yet just over a year on from signing for Arsenal, Madueke has a league title winners medal (‘while others are tweeting and posting’) with 25 starts to his name last season, 16 of which were in the Premier League.

In reality, being Bukayo Saka’s third leg has, to this point, proved to be a savvy career move for Madueke because he is getting plenty of time on the pitch in Saka’s increasing absences. This extends to the England National Team too, where Madueke plays the same role. But it was a role that still earned him four starts for his country in a World Cup, including a start in the quarter-final against Norway.

A Premier League title winners medal, a Champions League Final appearance and four World Cup starts was not a bad return for Madueke in terms of playing time. I think we knew when Arsenal bought him that Noni was a talented but phlegmatic player, relentless in taking on his full-back but the quality of his end-product could vary markedly.

In his new signing profile of Madueke on Arseblog, Phil Costa wrote, ‘there’s a feeling that Arsenal lack penetration from their wingers (Bukayo Saka aside); chaos factor, some unpredictability, and Madueke brings this in spades. His first thought when receiving the ball is centred around provoking defenders and driving towards goal, which means you can isolate him without too much focus on the overall setup – you just wind him up and let him go.

‘There are two specific metrics to love when assessing the 23-year-old; per FBRef data, he currently sits in the 95th percentile for progressive carries (6.82 per 90) and the 98th percentile for carries into the box (4.12 per 90). Those are big numbers.’ There was never any doubt about Madueke’s ability to get the ball into threatening areas, the question has always been what he does when he gets there.

Last season, some clips of him harumphing the ball out of the stadium on his right foot went semi-viral. I also think some of his performances were impacted by a lack of balance in the front three. With technicians like Havertz and Odegaard unavailable, he was often playing alongside fellow blunderbusses like Gyokeres and Martinelli.

I admit that my tolerance for inefficiency is high when it comes to attackers. I think attacking is a volume game. The vast majority of attacks come to nothing, the vast majority of shots do not go in or even work a goalkeeper. Individual attacks are the weather but, overall, attacking is the climate. The more you do it and sustain it, the more likely you are to score.

So my ‘we can fix him’ gene for slightly wayward wingers is high. I didn’t even mind Gervinho (a frustrating player, no doubt, but the Bradford miss has become the defining image of his Arsenal career which I don’t believe was fully representative of his performances).

The video of Madueke’s right foot ballooning the ball into the upper tier against Kairat last season has been refined. Both his goals this season have been on his right foot, particularly notably against Nottingham Forest where he cut in on his right and unleashed a low and controlled shot. It might have taken a helpful deflection but that’s because he kept the attempt low.

Last season, his right footed efforts were more in danger of colliding with low flying aircraft on their way into orbit. Noni’s goal against Slavia Praha demonstrated his pace in behind. It was the sort of goal and chance Gabriel Martinelli was hoovering up in Europe last season. European games tend to offer more space in behind and with Martinelli gone, Madueke is one of the few Arsenal attackers explosive enough to exploit it.

Indeed, in my view, he ought to have won Arsenal a match winning penalty in Budapest against Paris Saint Germain in May. There are signs of greater maturity and efficiency in his game. According to WhoScored.com his pass success rate in the Premier League last season was 76.2%. This season so far it is 86.3%.

I think he has learned that he does not have to go for the full-back at 100mph every single time he gets the ball and has varied his game. In the Champions League game against Lille, he sent 15 crosses into the penalty area, having sent six into the area in the game before against Leeds. 15 crosses sounds like a lot but it was very clearly under instruction from Mikel Arteta.

After that Lille game, the manager said of Madueke, ‘I said when you talk about players being ‘clinical’, sometimes that means scoring five in every 100. It’s about generating volume, more actions and getting him into the good positions, because he will decide matches. He had a really big contribution a few days ago, today he had a contribution in the last final pass as well.’

Being omitted from the England squad in September, according to Arteta, provided additional motivation for Noni, ‘After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him.’

He has now been omitted from the England squad again for the November international round. It is a decision I don’t really understand from Thomas Tuchel but I am happy if it continues to provide Madueke with an additional reason to fine tune his game and because it hopefully protects a player who has become very important.

I admit I am not entirely sure how good Madueke is going to be in, say, three years’ time. He is 24 and it’s at that age that attackers typically start to increase their decisive actions. He has Max Dowman in the rearview mirror too. I think Madueke has a really high ceiling and there are small, but encouraging, signs of improvement.

#1727. Opinion: Liverpool are getting back a world-class player, that's confirmed

Liverpool are getting a world-class player back after the international break. That's just confirmed at this point.

The international break is nearly over. Liverpool are back in action at the weekend and it's a massive one to say the least - Manchester United at Anfield.

Not just any United side, either, but a new-look one under Mauricio Pocchetino. The Argentine has taken over from Michael Carrick and this, incredibly, will be his debut in the dugout.

It's difficult to know what Liverpool should expect as a result of that. United could be re-inspired or it could be their 14th consecutive false dawn - we just can't be sure.

What we can be sure of, though, is that the Reds look like they'll be returning from the break in good form. One player, in particular, looks world-class.

Florian Wirtz has been hit-and-miss since joining Liverpool. Mainly miss, if we're honest.

But there's no question that he's one of the world's most talented footballers and the problem has always been that Liverpool can't get the best out of him. Certainly, they view him as a generational talent in Germany and that's what the Reds thought they were buying.

They were right, too. Wirtz is exactly that - you've just got to get the most out of him to do that. It's the same for any elite footballer, too.

If you don't put them in an environment to succeed, you won't see their elite level. The margins at the top are too fine that it's virtually impossible to stand out if things aren't setup well for you.

This season, though, we're beginning to see more of Wirtz's best. He's had some brilliant moments and ran some victories for Liverpool. We just need to see it more consistently.

It seems obvious, too, that last season sapped Wirtz of his confidence. It was, after all, the first time in his career that he didn't exceed expectations. It's difficult to know how a player reacts to that and the German retreated into himself a bit.

It's telling, for instance, that Jurgen Klopp has made it his mission to build that confidence back up since taking over the German National Team.

“I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time,” said Klopp after Germany beat the Netherlands 4-0.

“An extraordinary footballer. We have also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he is so vocal. He is the first pressing player, can press two players without getting tired.”

Wirtz is reacting to that confidence building very well, too. He was outstanding against the Dutch, scoring twice and with both goals demanding elite quality.

It was the performance of a world-class player and we're confident that Klopp's plan is working. He's sending a player full of confidence back to Liverpool and with that, the Reds are getting a genuine superstar.

Now it's their turn to keep Wirtz's momentum going.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to information from 4-4-2.ch, clubs in both Serie A and the Premier League are seriously considering a move for the 24-year-old midfielder, who started last night in Switzerland’s 4-0 win over Scotland and impressed.

Roma, Juventus, Atalanta and Como are the four Italian clubs that are looking at the Swiss international. From England, it is Aston Villa and Nottingham Forest that are monitoring his situation closely.

#1724. Attacking efficiency key for Hull’s visit

Arsenal are in Premier League action this afternoon, taking on Hull City at home. No doubt there will be some rotation from the midweek Champions League game, with players like Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes, Myles-Lewis-Skelly, Jurrien Timber, Riccardo Calafiori, Christos Tzolis and Kai Havertz all potential inclusions. I wrote yesterday about Viktor Gyokeres and whether his good performance in midweek would see him keep his place. On the Swedish international, Mikel Arteta said:

I think everybody was so happy to see, not only the goals but also the performance, how free he looked, how happy he looked, the energy that he could transmit on that football pitch. That’s exactly what we need, that’s what we’re signing, that’s the type of player that can help us to make the difference and he certainly did that during the night.

So let’s see if that means he keeps his place up front. Noni Madueke has had a decent couple of weeks too, with the manager revealing he’d used the elongated Interlull in October to up the ante in terms of his own training:

What he did is he went abroad and he trained. He got somebody to train him and he went into a programme, he wanted to do that. That’s Noni and that’s his mindset – he wants to get better. I love that action that he took because at that moment he wasn’t playing.

With Bukayo Saka injured and Max Dowman suspended until after the Newcastle game, he’s more or less the only option on the right-hand side, so fingers crossed he can continue that form today against a team who are likely to try and make life difficult for us. Players who can beat a man and find some space are really valuable for fixtures like this, and he might prove very important later on.

Hull started the season brightly, but haven’t won since the end of August. All the same, five draws from their last seven games tells you they’re a relatively tough nut to crack, and with a back five they’ll surely have looked at how other teams have come to our place to frustrate us. An early goal is always useful, Ezri Konsa’s quick strike against Everton probably prevented that game from being as much of a slog as it might have been, but we might also need some patience today too.

Some of the difficult games they’ve come through and competed in, they’ve earned the right to be here and been impressive. We’ve been discussing that with the boys on what to expect from them tomorrow and to be clear on what we need to do to beat them.

Arsenal were a bit wasteful in midweek against Slavia Prague, and so making the most of our chances will be important today. Whether it’s Gyokeres or Havertz, and regardless of the construction of the midfield, we need to be more clinical as a team in general, so let’s hope we can produce that today. I take nothing for granted in this league, but hopefully this is one we can just deal with as efficiently as possible before we head into the Interlull.

I just want to mention the launch of The 22 we had at Big Red last night, a huge thanks to everyone who came along and bought a book. The reaction to it was fantastic, and it was real pleasure to meet so many of you. A massive thanks too to Martin and Louise and all the staff there who were such a great help – with the Tollington closed for a while, Big Red is open today if you’re looking for your pre-game pints.

The last batch of books will go on general sale today at 6pm (UK time) via this link (which will be live at that time): https://www.yumastudios.com/store/p/the-22

Orders are limited to two per person, and once they sell out, that’s it. This is a real collector’s item, and the best of luck if you’re after one.

#1723. Real Madrid star Arda Guler rewarded for what is set to be his best campaign yet

By Matt Law | 18 Nov 2026 15:06, Last updated: 18 Nov 2026 15:07

Real Madrid have announced that Arda Guler has signed a new contract at Bernabeu until the end of the 2031-32 campaign.

The Turkey international made the move to Bernabeu from Fenerbahce in the summer of 2023, and he has represented the capital giants on 126 occasions, scoring 22 goals and registering 32 assists in the process.

Guler has started the campaign with four goals and seven assists in 14 appearances in all competitions, including three goals and five assists in 12 La Liga outings.

Real Madrid have announced that the 21-year-old has agreed a new deal in the Spanish capital until the summer of 2032.

"Real Madrid C. F. and Arda Guler have agreed to extend the contract of our player, who will remain linked to the club until June 30, 2032," read a statement from the capital giants.

Guler has started 10 of Real Madrid's 12 La Liga matches this season, demonstrating his importance for Los Blancos, although he has only played in two of their four Champions League league stage fixtures this term.

The playmaker missed the team's 2026-27 European opener against Inter Milan through suspension, while he was rested against AEK Athens in their last game in the competition.

Guler has not scored more than six times in a campaign for Real Madrid since his arrival, but he is already just two goals off that total in November.

Real Madrid won La Liga and the Champions League during Guler's first campaign at the club, but he only featured on 12 occasions in 2023-24.

Guler has won five trophies during his time at Bernabeu, but this could be his best campaign yet both from a personal and team point of view.

Guler is expected to be in the starting team when Real Madrid continue their La Liga campaign against Celta Vigo on November 21.

The playmaker will then be hoping to make his third Champions League appearance of the season when Los Blancos face PSV Eindhoven in the competition on November 24.

#1722. Report: Liverpool send scouts to watch South American sensation in action

Liverpool have had quite a lot of luck when it comes to signing South America players.

Right now, the Reds have Alisson, Ronald Araujo and Alexis Mac Allister among their ranks and, so far this season, all three of them have played fairly regular roles for Liverpool.

Obviously, the same can't be said for all South American's with Darwin Nunez's poor performances probably the most recent flop in that regard.

However, more often than not, the Reds' eye for talent in South America has been top notch and, with Luis Diaz and Nunez being sold last summer, Liverpool lost a decent chunk of them.

But, fortunately for the Reds, it now looks like they're trying to rectify that with the latest update to emerge from Anfield being rather exciting.

Liverpool have cast their eyes on Athletico Paranaense's Arthur Dias

One of the main things Liverpool have tried to do with their squad over the summer is get them prepared for the future.

The Anfield outfit have always had one of the best academies in the world but, signing young talent from other clubs has also been a key part to their recruitment strategy.

Trey Nyoni and Rio Ngumoha are the best examples of this right now but, after the upcoming transfer windows, that could be about to change.

That is, if an update from FussballEuropa is to be believed.

"Liverpool FC has its eyes everywhere – including on the Brazilian market. The Reds' scouts are keeping a close eye on Arthur Dias. The race for the talented center-back is already on," they wrote.

Athletico Paranaense could have made a significant sum from Arthur Dias last summer. Tottenham Hotspur showed concrete interest and reportedly submitted an offer of just over €20 million. However, this was too low for Paranaense, and consequently, no deal was reached.

Dias is one of the most exciting defensive talents in Brazilian football and, at just 19 years old, has developed into an indispensable defensive leader at Paranaense. And not only that: Dias has even earned two caps for the Brazilian national team.

"This automatically makes the rising star a target for other clubs. According to information from Fussballeuropa.com, Premier League side Liverpool are keeping a close eye on Dias. The Reds are regularly monitoring the young defender and keeping a close eye on his development."

Arthur Dias could plug the gap in Liverpool's defence

Obviously, the future of Liverpool's defence is up in the air at the moment.

Nobody knows what the Reds' plans for their players who's contracts expire are and, that is a tad concerning.

Three of their defenders are set to leave L4 in June 2027 and, if a deal isn't reached before then, they'll be able to exit for nothing.

This has now happened two years in a row with Trent Alexander-Arnold and Ibrahima Konate both leaving for free.

Liverpool's lack of knowing is probably why so many defenders are still being linked.

Dias is only 19 years old and, he may have only featured in 55 professional games across his career thus far but, this season alone, he's played 31 times in the Brazilian Serie A and has even scored a goal.

Obviously, he's still very young so he has a lot of developing to do but, from the fact that he's played all of those games in the Brazilian Serie A already, it's clear that he's one to watch.

And, with Virgil van Dijk, Kostas Tsimikas, Joe Gomez and Ronald Araujo all potentially leaving, Dias could definitely be on Liverpool's shortlist.

#1721. Arsenal 1-0 Hull: Not efficient, but enough

In yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points. In yesterday’s game against Hull, Arsenal took 21 shots, 10 of which were on target, and scored one goal from that. Efficient?

Despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play. Passes weren’t quite quick enough or accurate enough, but there were moments when we could have found the breakthrough. Gabriel almost got on the end of a Noni Madueke cross which was flicked on towards the back post, Rice had a tame shot from a free kick before a late header which he probably should have done better with.

And then there was Kai Havertz. It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper. I haven’t seen replays but in real time I felt like he should have pulled the trigger – instead he over-complicated it. You have to be prepared to shoot from there, even if it’s on your wrong foot.

Then there was a penalty incident when he complained vociferously, play went on, the ref was then told to go to the screen and we all assumed it would be a penalty. However, the ref said it was a foul but Havertz was offside – and it felt like a massive waste of time. Afterwards, it emerged it should have been a penalty, but apparently the rule is ‘open to interpretation’. So clear as mud then.

In the second half, we seemed to play down our right a lot, with Madueke the outlet most of the time. I thought he did pretty well, much better than Christos Tzolis on the other side, but the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Mikel Merino replaced Rice (who seemed to be on the end of a wild challenge in midfield that the ref just ignored as he tumbled through the air), and Viktor Gyokeres came on for Havertz.

On 71 minutes though, we found the goal. Madueke’s shot was spilled by the keeper, Odegaard was quickest to react to poke the ball home for 1-0. And to be fair, you always felt confident that would be enough. We are the masters of the single goal margin win, and this was another one. Not a day that will live long in the memory or anything, but a 1-0 win that takes us into the Interlull in really good shape, and there’s not much arguing with that.

Or really, much more to say about this game. Mikel Arteta sounded happy enough, saying:

I’m delighted with the win. To go into the international break with a win is one of the best things about being a coach or player, I would say. Regarding the performance, I thought we were the better team, had enough chances to score and make it bigger for ourselves and we weren’t efficient enough to take them.

We then had to rely on generating volume, plenty of persisting until we finally broke them down. Martin then got the goal. Not the most beautiful one, but the most effective one, a simple ‘shoot and then follow the next action’, and that was ultimately enough to win the game.

So Arsenal sit top of the table, with 9 wins from 10 so far this season in the league, and it’s a very impressive run of form. Do I wish we had more attacking potency? Absolutely, and I do worry a bit that it might bite us in the arse somewhere down the line, but for now, we can see that this is a team that just knows how to win, and perhaps that’s the most important thing.

Right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. I have to head back to Dublin today. It was great to see lots of you over the weekend, until next time! And we’ll have an Arsecast Extra for you tomorrow too.

#1720. Antonio Rudiger compares Kylian Mbappe to Cristiano Ronaldo in Real Madrid defence

By Naim Beneddra | 18 Nov 2026 15:20

Real Madrid defender Antonio Rudiger has launched a passionate defence of Kylian Mbappe's contribution to the team, drawing a striking comparison with Cristiano Ronaldo, Karim Benzema and Gareth Bale to challenge criticism of the Frenchman's defensive work.

Mbappe has been one of Madrid's most prolific players since arriving from Paris Saint-Germain in 2024, reaching 100 goals for the Spanish giants despite their struggles to win major silverware over the past two seasons.

However, his extraordinary goalscoring record has not prevented questions being raised about his willingness to press opponents and contribute when Madrid are out of possession.

The issue has become particularly prominent under Jose Mourinho, whose demanding approach requires his players to maintain their defensive organisation.

Rudiger believes some of those expectations are misplaced, arguing that a forward of Mbappe's quality should be judged primarily on his ability to decide matches.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with The Athletic, the former Chelsea centre-back questioned whether it made sense to demand the same defensive responsibilities from a player who has already delivered 100 goals for Madrid.

"Should I tell Mbappe [...] to do my job? It makes no sense," Rudiger said.

The German then pointed to one of the most successful attacking partnerships in Real Madrid's history to explain his position.

Rudiger believes Madrid's previous success offers an important lesson about how to accommodate outstanding attacking players.

He recalled the celebrated partnership of Ronaldo, Bale and Benzema, who spearheaded the club's attack during a period that produced four Champions League titles between 2014 and 2018.

The trio were renowned for their individual attacking qualities and ability to deliver decisive moments in major matches.

Rudiger suggested that Madrid did not achieve those successes by constantly scrutinising their forwards' defensive contributions.

He pointed to the achievements of the three players before insisting that discussion of attackers should not always revolve around their work without the ball.

His argument is particularly relevant to Mbappe, whose goals have frequently provided Madrid with a decisive advantage even when the team's collective performances have attracted criticism.

The French international has continued to deliver exceptional numbers in front of goal, although Madrid have struggled to translate his individual productivity into the trophies expected at the Santiago Bernabeu.

Rudiger's comments do not suggest that Mbappe should be exempt from defensive responsibilities. Rather, the defender believes the rest of the team must find an effective balance around players whose greatest value comes in attacking positions.

The comparison with Ronaldo is especially significant given the Portuguese forward's standing at Madrid, where he scored 450 goals in 438 appearances and helped establish an era of sustained European dominance.

Mbappe has already been compared to Ronaldo following his spectacular individual performances for Madrid, but Rudiger has approached the comparison from a different perspective.

For the experienced defender, the question is how Madrid can create the conditions for their most influential attackers to flourish.

Rudiger also addressed another recurring criticism of Madrid's squad: the difficulty of managing a dressing room filled with established international stars.

The 33-year-old acknowledged that the club's collection of strong personalities can create challenges for any manager.

He referred to Rafael Benitez and Julen Lopetegui, whose spells in charge of Madrid ended prematurely, as examples of coaches who encountered similar difficulties.

"It's not a myth. That's the reality," Rudiger admitted when discussing the influence of big personalities at the club.

His comments offer an insight into the environment Mourinho has inherited since returning to Madrid during the summer.

The Portuguese manager has been tasked with restoring the club's success after two seasons without a major trophy, with Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius Junior among the players expected to lead that recovery.

Rudiger spoke positively about Mourinho's influence, revealing that the manager had contacted him towards the end of last season to explain his plans and express his desire to keep the German at the club.

He also described a lighter side to Mourinho's personality, explaining that the former Manchester United and Chelsea boss enjoys telling jokes in the dressing room while maintaining a far more demanding approach on the training pitch.

The defender extended his support to Vinicius, who has experienced a difficult start to the season and faced increased competition for his position.

Rudiger insisted that the Brazilian continues to work hard to improve his performances and remains an important figure in Madrid's plans.

Vinicius has recently rediscovered his goalscoring form with Brazil, scoring five times across two international friendlies against Japan and Singapore.

His return presents Mourinho with another selection decision as Madrid prepare to resume their domestic campaign.

For Rudiger, however, the responsibility for restoring Madrid's success cannot rest solely on the willingness of Mbappe, Vinicius or Bellingham to defend.

His comparison with Ronaldo's celebrated attacking partnership reflects a broader conviction that Madrid must find a collective structure capable of making the most of their attacking talent.

“When David Silva was here, everyone was worried - Kevin [De Bruyne] arrived. When Sergio Agüero was here, everyone was worried – Erling [Haaland] arrived. When Ferdinando left, Rodri arrived. It’s just about this.

Maresca added: “Hopefully we can do the things that we need to do. It doesn’t help that there are players that for different reasons want to leave, this is for sure.

“It’s normal, I’m not worried about that. When the transfer window closes and we have all the squad there, for sure it will be different.”

#1718. Strops, scruff, and chaos

I watched Man Utd v Aston Villa last night. When Villa conceded late on to let a two goal lead slip for the second time in the game, Unai Emery threw a strop and went down the tunnel. It’s not the first time he’s eschewed a handshake with the opposition manager, and his post-game interview where he insisted he thought the game was over was very funny because it was such obvious bullshit.

This is someone who has managed over 1000 games in his career. I’m pretty sure he knows when the final whistle blows and when it doesn’t. Can you imagine if Mikel Arteta did that? You wouldn’t be able to move for all the opinion pieces about what a sore loser he is and all the rest. But perhaps Emery gets a pass because he is ‘the best manager in the league’. Anyway, perhaps it provides a stay of execution for Michael Carrick at Man Utd, which can only be a good thing.

Meanwhile, it looks as if Pierre Sage is gonna get fired by Crystal Palace and replaced by Thomas Frank. That seems a sensible appointment to me. Enough time has passed since his spell at Sp*rs for the toxins to wear off, and he’s clearly a good manager. I’ve never been convinced by Sage, I just think he looks too scruffy. As if someone got a 10 year old to draw man and brought it to life.

I quite enjoyed this quote from Mikel Arteta in his post-game press conference after Saturday’s 1-0 win over Hull:

Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game.

I love it as a concept, adding some chaos to our control makes a lot of sense, but it also kinda seems at odds with what the manager asks of his players. Maybe he just means more shots from distance, maybe riskier pass when we’re trying to break the opposition down, or maybe there’s something he’s got cooking for over the Interlull and when we return we see something we never expected. He did kick the shit out of a dugout chair on Saturday, that’s a new enough development to be fair.

I wonder was he referring to the Kai Havertz chance in the first half, when he could have shot on his right foot but tried to cut back/lay it off. If you shoot, maybe you don’t score but as we saw with the winning goal from Martin Odegaard, it might end up in the path of another Arsenal player who can finish it off. Perhaps too there’s a bit of a through line between being more chaotic and what Noni Madueke is doing at the moment. He can be a bit scattergun, but as Nick Wright points out on Sky Sports, his numbers are improving. I don’t think Arteta will ever embrace full chaos, all the time, but if he can add a little more to the mix, it could certainly help.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. A bit shorter than normal, I know. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. #1717. More than just a football club: Cardinale’s vision to make AC Milan a multi-billion empire

In case you weren’t aware from his repeatedly bold comments in the media, Gerry Cardinale has big plans for AC Milan.

The RedBird Capital founder and chief has made one concept very clear: while he is at the helm, Milan are no longer just a football club, but a platform that aims to integrate sports, infrastructure, and entertainment. Of course AC Milan will be at the centre of the web, but the idea is to expand.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The proof of this comes from a three-letter acronym: MSE. It stands for Milan Sports & Entertainment and it is the new holding company created by RedBird. The idea, simply put, is to bring together investments and activities in various sectors under one umbrella.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport recall, Cardinale explained to the Financial Times that the assets involved could be valued in the mid-single-digit billions, meaning several billion dollars. So, how does he plan to get there?

Cardinale linked the creation of MSE to the process initiated with the acquisition of Milan: “Milan Sports & Entertainment is the culmination of this work and of what we have built since we first invested in the club four years ago.”

In his interview with La Gazzetta, Cardinale clarified that the new structure is also created to support the Rossoneri’s sporting ambitions: “The driving force behind operations like this is to provide Milan with the financial strength needed to compete in the transfer market and secure the best players in the world.”

There are examples of this kind of model working already. Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, AEG and Fenway Sports Group are among the most prominent and – given his background in the USA – Cardinale knows each of them well.

According to CNBC valuations, KSE was worth $26.05bn in 2026, FSG $15.37bn, and AEG $11.99bn in 2025, excluding music and hotel businesses.

KSE boasts franchises such as the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche and Arsenal, as well as venues such as SoFi Stadium, Ball Arena, and Emirates Stadium. The group combines sports, infrastructure and real estate development such as Hollywood Park, the district built around SoFi Stadium.

AEG – founded by Philip Anschutz – have instead built its model on the management and development of venues. It owns or manages venues such as Crypto.com Arena and The O2 in London plus the Los Angeles Kings and LA Galaxy, and operates in concert promotion and ticketing. The LA LIVE project developed around Crypto.com Arena puts the venue at the centre of a greater ecosystem.

Fenway Sports Group – born around the Boston Red Sox and Liverpool FC – have developed a holding company with interests in media, marketing, real estate, and entertainment. It’s a model Cardinale knows first hand: in 2021, RedBird invested approximately $750m in FSG, acquiring a stake of around 11%, based on an enterprise valuation of $7.35bn.

MSE in theory can harness elements of all three of these experiences: KSE’s integration of sports and infrastructure, AEG ‘s commercial development of facilities and FSG ‘s multi-sport approach. The main difference is the purpose declared by Cardinale: to use all of it to funnel money back into Milan.

From the stadium shared with Inter to the possibility of an arena in San Donato, including the new NBA Europe venture and even tennis: MSE’s scope includes various initiatives that go beyond the playing field.

The main infrastructure project is the future Generali Stadium, the new 71,500-seat facility designed by Foster + Partners and Manica. Developed jointly by the two Milanese clubs, it represents a key element of the transformation of the San Siro area and will not be a Rossoneri-only facility.

The promoters intend for the stadium to host year-round activities, from matches to concerts, as well as catering, events, and hospitality services. In other words, like the stadiums and arenas mentioned above, it will become more than just a place to go for two hours on a Sunday.

In San Donato Milanese, RedBird are also considering the possibility of building a 20,000-seat arena. Cardinale explained that the fund already owns the land and has planning permission, but the idea is also linked to Milan’s potential involvement in NBA Europe. Another area of ​​focus concerns tennis, with the possibility of hosting a tournament in the city.

Finally, RedBird intend to develop a company dedicated to managing stadiums and arenas, with services including catering, merchandising and premium hospitality. The goal is to build commercial expertise to apply to the facilities connected to the group, but also to make it available to other owners and sports clubs.

This phase will be co-ordinated by Brett Yormark, appointed CEO of MSE and set to step down as head of the Big 12 (a conference in College Football) at the end of January 2027. He worked for 14 years at Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, overseeing the development of the Brooklyn Nets and the Barclays Center. He has also gained experience in NASCAR and Roc Nation.

The choice to go for Yormark reflects the desire to entrust the platform to someone with expertise across multiple different fields in the sporting and commercial worlds.

All these grand plans are well and good, but how will ideas turn into money that drives AC Milan forward? MSE’s economic potential is measured not only through the club’s revenues, but also through the activities that RedBird intends to develop around sports, infrastructure and entertainment.

The starting point is obviously Milan as a club, which closed the 2025-26 financial year with revenues of €464.6m, over €100m of which came from sponsorships. The main infrastructure opportunity is the new San Siro, an investment of approximately €2.3bn shared with Inter.

Projections contained in the design documents indicate a potential annual revenue of approximately €120.4m for the facility as a whole (both for the Rossoneri and the Nerazzurri), through sporting, commercial, and complementary services

These are numbers that will be revised upwards by the two clubs when considering, for example, the record agreement with Generali for naming rights. It is worth a total of €650m over 25 years, divided into €10m per year for the first five years and €30m per season for the following 20, once the stadium is built.

One of the areas on which RedBird Capital are focusing most is hospitality, which is currently worth around €15m per year for the Rossoneri. The international benchmark has already been set by Legends Global, a company Cardinale knows well.

Legends are what the Milan owner sees as a model for developing premium services, restaurants, and commercial spaces. The most obvious example is at FC Barcelona: with the support of LG, the club have marketed nearly 5,000 VIP seats at Camp Nou, generating over €380m in contracted revenue.

They aim to generate another €700m through multi-year licenses for an additional 2,000 seats. This isn’t annual revenue, but rather contracts spread over 15 or 30 years, so a guaranteed flow of money coming in that Cardinale aims to replicate.

Another agreement which demonstrates the potential of this kind of arrangement is the one with Real Madrid for the Santiago Bernabéu. It involves an investment of approximately €360m in exchange for 20-year participation in some of the stadium’s businesses,.

Legends Global also operate in facilities and events management. Following the acquisition of ASM Global (who actually proposed renovating San Siro for non-football events in Italy) in 2024, the group claims a presence in over 450 venues, approximately 20,000 events, and 165 million guests annually. Their European partnerships include Arsenal, Chelsea and Porto.

FC Barcelona launches new VIP seating licenses at Spotify Camp Nou with Legends Global

🔗 More details: https://t.co/awtEsnYE6X pic.twitter.com/iCMuM0QD35

— FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) September 25, 2026

To illustrate the potential it could hold for Italy as a whole, the English subsidiary reported revenues of £131.6m in 2024, of which £105.5m came from facility and event management and £26.1m from catering. Before the integration with ASM Global, Legends had reported revenues of $1.7bn in the period ending in March 2024, with 67% coming from food and beverage sales.

In Italy, a benchmark is Forumnet, who in 2024 generated €29.7m in revenue and €12.8m in EBITDA (Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation). They manage the Assago Forum which hosts approximately 60-70 concerts a year, demonstrating how a venue can generate activity well beyond the sports calendar.

As mentioned, an arena is being planned in San Donato with an estimated investment of around €400m, which could become the basis for a Milanese franchise in NBA Europe. For reference, Olimpia Milano – the current basketball team in the city – generate around €15m through ticketing, season tickets, sponsorships and merchandising.

For NBA Europe, projections speak of over $1.5bn to be distributed to the clubs in the first six years. A theoretical division among the 12 permanent franchises would equate to approximately $20.8m per team per year, but this is not fixed yet. Entry costs – estimated by the media to be between $500m and over $1bn – also remain to be determined.

Tennis represents another potential area for development. The ATP 500 in Halle generates around €5m in revenue, excluding television rights, while the ATP Finals in Turin generate around €60m. These are events with different dimensions and scopes, but they provide a scale.

The creation of MSE has a stated objective: to strengthen Milan’s financial capacity and reduce the gap with the richest clubs on the international scene, particularly those in the Premier League.

The gap is also evident when comparing revenues. AC Milan closed the 2025-26 season with €464.6m, a significant result considering their absence from European competitions , but still far from the top English clubs.

According to the Deloitte Football Money League, in the 2024-25 season, Liverpool generated €836.1m, Arsenal €821.7m and Manchester United €793.1m. Tottenham and Chelsea also exceeded €670m and €580m, respectively.

The comparison covers different financial years, but it still shows the magnitude of the gap. Liverpool generated revenues equal to approximately 1.8 times those of Milan, while Chelsea recorded a turnover approximately €120 higher.

The chasm shows how clubs in the Premier League have showcased an ability to generate commercial revenue, enhance stadiums and reach a global audience. The gap has only been growing, and TV rights will be another focus, though that is outside of just Cardinale’s hands.

Speaking of the owner, it is now obvious he sees MSE as the name that will house the tools to try build a real sporting and commercial world around Milan. It remains to be seen how effective it will be, but the starting point is there.
